On the orders of the day:
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to rise to a question of
Maple Products

privilege. I hold in my hand a oo-py of the Ottawa Citizen for this morning, December 11, on the front page of which appears an article written by Torchy Anderson, Citizen parliamentary writer. This article is headed "Leader S. Low Seems Facing Party 'Revolt' ", and goes on to say:
Following last night's abortive effort to advance legislation by which Canada would participate in Bretton Woods financial undertakings, corridor rumour had it that Solon Low, Social Credit Leader, faced something of * revolt within the ranks of his party. It was said that as late as yesterday afternoon Mr. Low had assured other leaders that the first stage of the debate could be finished.
My point of privilege is this: In the first place, Solon Low does not face any threat of party revolt. I endorse completely the action that was taken by hon. members who were speaking, asking questions and tiying to get information here until eleven o'clock last night. I repeat that I endorse that completely.
Secondly, I did not at any time give any undertaking to anybody that the debate could be finished. I have repeatedly assured the leaders of other groups that I would do my best to see that the business of the house was advanced-and I am doing my best. But at the same time I am trying to do my best for the people of this country. And I want it definitely known that the writer of this article is -trying has level best to read something into the actions of this group that he has no right to read into them.
Furthermore, when anybody in any article of this kind tries to impress upon the public that the Social Credit group is engaged in a filibuster for the assured purpose of blocking the business of this house, that is not true. I wish it definitely known that thus far this group has questioned only six out of the twenty-six articles in the Bretton Woods agreement, and there are hundreds of questions remaining that could be asked with respect to it.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, December 10, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair:
That it is expedient to present a measure to grant authority to accept on behalf of Canada and to carry out the obligations of Canada under the articles of agreement for an international monetary fund and an international bank for reconstruction and development prepared by the united nations monetary and financial conference held at Bretton Woods in July, 1944; to authorize the payment of the subscriptions required from Canada out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund to an amount not exceeding seven hundred million dollars; and to authorize the borrowing under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, of sums not exceeding seven hundred million dollars.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure
that all hon. members hope to be clear of the woods before long. I come from the prairies and quite frankly I admit that I shall be glad to get out of the woods and back to the prairies. It has been suggested that we have been trying to obstruct this measure, but I would point out that if we were we could quite easily do it until the new year. We have raised questions on only about six articles, and there are thirty-one. We could ask questions on every single one of those articles, and then in addition there are the schedules. It cannot be said that we have received answers to all the questions that we have asked at this stage. When we are in the committee on banking and commerce we will be justified in asking for an explanation of every subsection of every section of every article; that is, a full explanation of just exactly what those sections and articles mean.
Just before eleven o'clock last night I was asking the minister if he would explain what section 4 article VIII means. I will read it to him so that he can get the purport of my question.
Section 4, article VIII reads:
Each member shall buy balances of its currency held by another member if the latter, in requesting the purchase, represents
(i)	that the balances to be bought have been recently acquired as the result of current transactions; or
(ii)	that their conversion is needed for making payments for current transactions.
This is the point. It goes on:
The buying member shall have the option to pay either in the currency of the member making the request or in gold.
If a nation had an unfavourable balance of trade it would not be able to pay in the currency of the other member nation and it must buy its own currency in gold. Where does it get the gold to buy that currency?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Would the hon. member go on with something else until I get that worked out? It is a complicated question.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I asked the minister yesterday afternoon this question:	Suppose the
fund has opened its doors for business, what difference would it make in the operation of the business of a country? Will it necessitate a gold basis or gold reserve? Would the minister say no?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
There is no question that it means that every nation will have to have a, gold reserve^ because it is compelled to buy
Bretton Woods Agreements

its own currency; therefore every nation must set up a gold reserve. Where are they going to get the gold if they have not got it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Where is there anything to say they have to pay in gold?	[DOT]

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
In section 4 of article VIII, which I have just read. It says:
The buying member shall have the option to pay either in the currency of the member making the request or in gold.
How can it get the currency of the member making the request except by trading with that nation, and if that nation refuses to buy
its goods it cannot get its currency and therefore it has to get gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: It would get the other nation's currency from the fund.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: If its quota is exhausted it cannot get it from the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: If it has exhausted its quota in the fund it does not have to do this.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Section 8 of article V deals with the question of a nation having exhausted its quota, in which case it cannot borrow any more from the fund. The nations that have its currency begin to get scared and they want to get rid of that nation's currency, and they demand payment, and the only way in which it could pay would be in gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Is not the answer found in section 4(v) of article VIII?

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: That is different.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: That is what the hon. gentleman is talking about-convertibility of foreign balances.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: You still have the difficulty that under section 8 of article V, when a member nation can no longer use the resources of the fund, it has to have gold. In view of the fact that there are several clauses in the articles of the fund requiring gold I think the minister will admit that for the successful operation of the fund each member must carry a reserve of gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: No, I do not admit that.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The minister will remember that when I started I said that I would try to prove that this was not merely a form of the old gold standard but that in many respects it was worse, and I will refer to the various reasons why I made that charge.
But first of all let me point out that no doubt the intention of the scheme is to try to provide for a redistribution of the large amount of gold that is held by the United States. I think the minister will agree with

that. A large amount of that gold will be made available to the various nations of the world. If the minister says no to that, we can only wait and see whether that is done, but I am satisfied that that is what will happen. There is no question that this fund will give the United States a very great power in the world, and its voting power will steadily expand, as its sales of currency increase and the voting power of other nations will decrease as they purchase United States currency. That is provided in the voting powers, so the ' United States will have a certain power when the fund comes into operation, and everything points to the fact that as time goes on that voting power will increase. If the United States had given an example to the world of how a country might be run on model lines, there might be some justification for suggesting that the United States should have greater power in the world to-day. But when we look back upon the record of the United States in between the two wars and remember the great amount of racketeering that took place therein, the extreme poverty which existed in many areas of the United States, especially among the sharecroppers-I think we shall have to admit that as an example-the United States cannot be the model upon which the whole world should be built. Until a nation has demonstrated to the world that it has set its own house in order and has shown how good conditions may be made available to all classes of its people, it can hardly contend that it is in a position to say how the world should be run.
As I pointed out to the minister when I first spoke in the committee stage, this is definitely a form of the gold standard, and in many ways worse. I should like to draw the minister's attention to these facts: article VII, subparagraph (ii) of section 2, provides that a nation, on demand by the fund, must buy gold when its currency is scarce, and that a nation, on demand by a nation holding its currency, must be prepared to sell gold-that is when currency is surplus. I say this is worse than the ordinary gold standard, for this reason. Severe penalties are imposed on nations when they get into a position where they have exceeded their quota and can no longer draw from the fund, i,vhen they have exceeded their right of drawing currency from the fund, and when their rat,e of interest has gone up to five per cent; and if a nation withdraws from the fund the other nations are pledged to discriminate to a certain extent against that nation. As to the extent to which they would discriminate, it is impossible to say; it will all depend on the conditions that exist at that time.

Bretton Woods Agreements

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: That is incorrect. There is no obligation to discriminate against that nation.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: It says that the members must not trade, on conditions other than the fund permits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Well, they shall not use that nation as-

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Contrary to the purpose
of the fund; if a withdrawing nation is operating contrary to the fund they cannot trade with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: That certainly is not so.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
It certainly is so. The
words "contrary to the fund" are there. If you want me to, I will read the whole thing again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
But it will not lead to
that conclusion, and it does not lead to discrimination.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
It cannot mean anything
else. Perhaps I had better read article XI;
Section 1. Each member undertakes:
(i)	Not to engage in nor to permit any of its fiscal agencies referred to in article V, section 1, to engage in, any transactions with a non-member or with persons in a non-member's territories which would be contrary to the provisions of this agreement or the purposes of the fund;
(ii)	Not to cooperate with a non-member or
with persons in a non-member's territories in practices which would be contrary to the provisions of this agreement or the purposes of the fund; and	-
(iii)	To cooperate with the fund with a view to the application in its territories of appropriate measures to prevent transactions with nonmembers or with persons in their territories which would be contrary to the provisions of this agreement or the purposes of the fund.
If the nation which has withdrawn has devaluated its currency without the right allowed by the fund, surely the action is contrary to the fund, and the nations will not trade with it, otherwise they would be trading in a currency which has been devaluated contrary to the intentions of the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Wait a minute. Is not
my hon. friend misreading that section entirely?

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: I don't think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: It is such a strained interpretation.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: A "strained"-?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
A strained-yes-and an
improper interpretation. This is the way he is reading the section: "Each member undertakes not to engage in nor to permit any of its fiscal agencies referred to in article V, section 1, to engage in any transactions with a non-member or with persons in a nonmember's territories which would be contrary to the provisions of this agreement or the purposes of the fund." He is reading it as if it means that the engaging in transactions would be contrary to the provisions of this agreement or the purposes of the fund, and that there is a provision against engaging in any transactions with a non-member or with persons in a non-member's territories. Now, that is not the true interpretation or construction of the section. The true interpre-ation is that a member is not to engage in transactions which would be contrary to the provisions of the agreement or the purposes of the fund. That is to say, if a country leaves the fund, the countries which belong to the fund have to carry on their original agreement with the fund and not engage in transactions with the member which would be contrary to the provisions of the agreement and the purposes of the fund. The people who stay in are not to use the member country that absents itself as a means of frustrating the purposes of the fund. It is simply a sort of avoidance of what might be called black market operations, contrary to the agreement which the party enters into. That is the true interpretation of the section. The "which" applies to transactions; it does not apply to engaging in transactions with the member.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Well, of course a great
deal rests on what the purpose of the fund is. But the fund considers it necessary to prevent a member from devaluating its currency, to maintain stabilization of exchange rates. Then surely it is obvious that, if a member is expelled from the fund because it devalues its currency, does not stabilize its rates of exchange, and if other members continue to trade with that member, they are helping to defeat the purpose of the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: The minister can say "no, no". He can say that black is white, but that does not make it white.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: That is why you want an international police force.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The other reason why I say that this condition is considerably worse than the gold standard is that the gold standard never provided for the setting up of an international authority which had powers in
Bretton Woods Agreements

excess of any powers of government, of any court of law, even apparently the international court of justice.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: What powers? They have not very many powers. The powers are extremely limited.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Every power on earth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I think you will find they have very great powers. When you remember how it was possible for the little mission that went to Australia in 1930 to compel that government to balance its budget and curtail its social services, merely through their monetary technique, if they could do it in those days, imagine what they can do under a set-up of this kind.
I think I have fully justified my argument when I say not only is it a form of the gold standard but in many respects it is infinitely worse.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Just to show how serious is the contention which the hon. member for Acadia is making, let me read the purposes of the fund. Where the trouble lies in this whole argument is that the people who are supporting this measure have never taken the trouble to interpret accurately the statements which are made in the various parts of the final act or to weigh the implications of the powers and stipulations which are found therein. As soon as they do they will realize how serious the situation is. Let me read the purposes of the fund and show how these would work out in the practical management of a nation, say under the present set-up we have in Canada:
The purposes of the international monetary fund are:
(i) To promote international monetary cooperation through a permanent institution which provides the machinery for consultation and collaboration on international monetary problems.
' Let me stop there and ask the minister this question. Suppose now that 'the very devices are .employed which are being used in Canada, or were used in the war, to bring down the cost of production of, we will say, any ordinary commodity. Let us suppose it is automobiles, or trucks, or anything of the kind; we know that the government has subsidized or relieved from tariff restrictions or in so^ne way aided manufacturers to get raw materials at a lower rate. Assume this kind of thing is done with the object of bringing down the cost of a particular commodity which is manufactured
[Mr. Quelch.J
in the country, thus enabling that commodity to be sold at a lower price than the corresponding commodity in another state.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: To be sold in Canada at a lower price?

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Either in Canada or outside. Or suppose it is just inside Canada. Bringing down the price of that commodity affects the value of the Canadian dollar, does it not?-because the lower the price of the commodity offered, the higher the value of the Canadian dollar, just as correspondingly the higher the price of goods the lower the value of the Canadian dollar. That simple device, which I think every member in this committee will recognize as a thoroughly legitimate one, could be interpreted as being contrary to this first purpose of the fund, because it would be said that there is no international monetary cooperation. Suppose Canada used her tremendous resources and began to use debt-free money, the possibilities of which I do not think the minister has even canvassed. Suppose she began to use debt-free money to subsidize the price of manufactured goods, bringing it down so as to produce price parity. She would certainly raise the value of the Canadian dollar, and that could be condemned by any body of people who were opposed to that idea as contrary to the purposes of number one, and the only absolute authority that could sit in judgment on that dispute would be the fund itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: They have no power to do anything about it.

maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Then what is all this agreement for, if they have no power to do something? What is the whole act for, if it does not give power to the fund to do something?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BRETTON WOODS AGREEMENTS
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND - INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT

of the world, as Japan was threatening to do, and as she would have done had she not been prevented by rigid quotas. Surely that would be interfering with the balanced growth of international trade. This is the provision with regard to which there has been the most discussion. Then take the next three:
To assist in the establishment of a multilateral system of payments in respect of current transactions between members and in the elimination of foreign exchange restrictions which hamper the growth of world trade.

The supreme court managed to destroy provincial autonomy completely, destroying the province's power over property and civil rights, since it declared ultra vires acts passed by the province with respect do property and civil rights. To my mind it does not make any difference what reason may be advanced for so doing. We have an example of that right now in Mr. Amery. I believe he was an honest man. He believed that the reasons he advanced for the actions he took were good reasons, and that what he did would be to the advantage of his country and of the world. It means a surrender of the sovereignty of this country. That is the reason why I am opposed to it, and the reason why I shall continue to be opposed to it.

It is now several days since' the resolution was passed , by the house and consideration of it begun in committee of the whole. Since that time we have had a long and sometimes interesting discussion in the committee. What I shall say I had planned to say before I knew what the hon. member for Peace River was going to say. I want to commend him for his action in the last few minutes. Up to that time the question before us was how much longer it would be wise for us to remain in committee of the whole discussing this subject. In this connection let me refer to two, matters which have been referred to by others in this house. There was a conference of leaders of different parties in this house a few days ago. It was suggesteid last night that it was there agreed that we would endeavour to get through the work of the session this week. That is true.
I want to say, however, with respect to the attitude of the Social Credit group, that the leader of that group did point out that one of the measures on which his associates would want to make a strong protest was the measure which is now before us. He specifically excepted that measure from any effort unduly to hurry up the work of the house.
Speaking for myself, and I think for many others in the house, I want to say that the discussion we have heard, led chiefly by the members of the Social Credit group, has been characterized by sincerity. It has all the evidence of thorough study. On their part I think a good deal of merit has been shown in the arguments they have brought forward. Having said that, I wish to say, one other thing. The Social Credit group has made its protest. There is no question that its members feel strongly on this subject. The protest has been well made. During more than two decades in another assembly in another part of Canada I have seen protests of this kind on several different occasions, and I do not remember one that was characterized by more sincerity or more evidence of study on the part of the group making it. Personally I want to commend the Social Credit members for presenting the other side of the story of the Bretton Woods measure.
It is obvious that the government wishes the measure to pass at this session; it is evident it is not disposed to postpone it. We supported the government on this resolution. .
While the arguments advanced by the Social Credit group have impressed us, they have not changed our minds. We still think that the balance of argument is in favour of the measure, in so far as its application to Canada is concerned.
Having said that, I again wish to commend the leader of the Social Credit group for not pressing this matter to the point where some arbitrary action on the part of the government would have to be taken. They have made a good case. It has impressed us all. They will have further opportunities to present their views. Their present action having been taken, we can now look forward to finding it possible to conclude our work this week.

It seems to me this is a question upon which members of the house will have to decide on balance. I do not think all will agree with everything contained in these long schedules. To do so would seem impossible. But I do believe that we must appraise this measure, both in committee and when it returns to the house, with balanced judgment. How much is good and how much is not so good? If the good outweighs that which we consider not so good, then the house should support the agreement.
So far as the international aspect of the matter is concerned, I wish to make it abundantly clear that I believe that any measure in the interests of the people of the world, in which Canada can participate for the good of the people of the world, ought to receive the support of this parliament. I do not take the view that international arrangements are bad; because I believe, even more certainly than I did a short time a^o, that responsible government at the international level must come ultimately-and the sooner it comes, the better for the peace of the world.

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, ,and to provide more particularly for an increase in the appropriation for loans and guarantees under part II of the act for the payment out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund of loans and losses in respect of loans, not exceeding in the aggregate one hundred and fifty million dollars, and in respect of guarantees, up to an aggregate principal amount of one hundred and twenty-five million dollars of investments guaranteed;
That under the said measure expenditures may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund to an aggregate amount not exceeding five million dollars incurred under or in carrying out the provisions of part V of the act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the main the amendments to the National Housing Act, 1944, which this resolution seeks authority to introduce, are of a technical nature, made necessary either by reason of ambiguities in the law or by recent developments which were not entirely foreseen when the act was drafted last year. They do not affect the underlying principles of the legislation. It was for this reason, and because of the need for immediate action, that the government felt justified in making several of the amendments effective by order in council under the War Measures Act before parliament assembled.
The amendments may be grouped under four general headings. First is a group of minor verbal changes which are necessary in order to clarify the intent of certain sections of the act. Most, though not all, of them were made effective by order in council P.C. 392, dated January 18, 1945.
Next is a group of amendments made effective by order in council P.C. 5794, dated August 30, 1945, which were necessary in order to clear the way for large-scale emergency operations by the life insurance companies in the field of rental housing. I referred to these when the bill creating the Central Mortgage
National Housing

and Housing Corporation was under discussion, and explained their general purpose. I shall give a detailed explanation, later when the clauses are reached in committee.
The third group of amendments relate to the appropriation sections, and, again, are in the nature of clarification rather than of modification in principle. They will be explained fully at a later stage. It is sufficient for me to say now that the enlargement of the appropiation under part II of the act removes certain unnecessarily rigid restrictions on operations under the act which had not been intended by the government, or, I think, by parliament. At present the $50 million appropriation under part II covers loans, losses and guarantees in respect of rental housing projects. To illustrate how inadequate this is I would point out that this appropriation would be insufficient should the full insurance companies' programme at present under consideration be approved. The appropriation has therefore been increased to $150 million to cover loans and losses. In addition, authority is given to guarantee investments up to $125 million, which is about the theoretical limit of life insurance companies' investments under the act. It is also proposed to appropriate $5 million under part V to provide a specific allotment of funds for housing research and community planning.
Finally, one amendment is being proposed arising out of the legislation creating the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which has the effect of permitting the delegation of certain of the powers of the Minister of Finance under the act to the new corporation when it is set up.
In conclusion, my suggestion is, if the house will accept it, that we spend very little time on the resolution, because I have the bill ready to introduce and it is not going to be possible for hon. members to give intelligent attention to our proposals unless they have before them a bill. We are at the stage where, it seems to me, the purposes of all would be best served if it goes to committee on the resolution, and the resolution is passed and given second reading. I may be given an opportunity to-day to introduce the bill; the bill will be distributed, then any questions can be raised on the second reading of the bill or in committee on the second reading of the bill, which will be taken up promptly. It cannot be taken up to-day because there should be an opportunity for hon. members to see it.

No, it carries a quotation from the Financial Post. I do not happen to have the Financial Post before me.
The government report on housing and community planning, brought down some time ago, states that in the lower income brackets the average income is $703 per family. On the basis of that income the maximum rent which should be paid, assuming that not more than twenty per cent of one's income should be applied to this purpose, is $12 per month, and in Canada we have not houses available in that income range. On page 115 of the same report are statistics, covering twelve metropolitan cities in Canada, showing that people in the lower income brackets should not be paying more than $11.72 per month, assuming they pay twenty per cent of their income, but they are paying $19 per month, which means that they are denying themselves food, clothing or health services to the extent of about $8 per month in order that they may have some place to live.
It has been found in almost every country in the world that the only way to provide housing for those in the lower income brackets is for the government or some government authority to step into the picture and make funds available over a long period of years at low rates of interest.
47696-207J
Previously I have discussed some of the housing projects in the United States, where the federal government has bridged the gap between the amount the individual can pay and what is an economic rent. I have described some of the beautiful apartments available in the city of Boston, where the rents range from $14 per month, which includes light and heat, for people receiving incomes of around six or seven hundred dollars a year. If you have an income of $1,300 a year you pay more. You pay according to your ability. But the federal authority has recognized that abolishing slums and providing congenial living quarters is a national objective which should have the support of all the people, and from a long-term point of view it is cheaper to eliminate these slums and give the people decent living quarters. In some of the public housing projects in the New York area, rents range from $8.43 in the Harlem river area, $8.42 in the Williamsburg district, $5.41 for the Red Hook houses, and $5.60 for the South Jamaica houses. The people living in these publicly-financed houses have incomes that range from $800 to $1,200, but those who live in the larger community have come to the conclusion that it is important for the future to wipe out these homes and provide more adequate houses.
All during the war I have tried to urge the administration to look forward and plan for our country, not only as far as the war effort was concerned but having regard to the future as well, by using a larger share of our raw material and man-power in providing houses for our people. I was able to cite statistics from the United States, compiled from the last war, to show how the efficiency of the people is reduced1 by workers being compelled to travel fifteen or twenty miles to work each day, and to carry on in the uncertainty of having living quarters. I found that in the city of Windsor, where the Secretary of State lives, some of the landlords were able to require the filling out of a questionnaire before anyone could come in. You had to prove that you were a Christian, that you did not talk too loudly, that you did not use your radio too much, that you had no children and no expectancy of any, that you did not use liquor, that you did not allow your guests to stay too late at night.
These were the conditions that prevailed all across Canada during the war, and1 the administration in my opinion failed to attach sufficient importance to the problem of providing houses for our people. Now we find ourselves with returning men who have been away for four or five years, some of them married before they left. They are coming home to
Veterans Affairs

their wives and families. Often the wife has been living with the family, and now these people feel, and rightly so, that they should have a place of their own to live in. I believe it was the member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt)-who distinguished himself by winning the Victoria Cross in this war-who found it so difficult to obtain living quarters that, as reported in the press, he felt that it might have been as well for him to remain away from the country. The situation is so critical that the minister at this stage Should make provision for an appropriation so that the money can be spent on building. A start should be made immediately to provide living quarters for the people in the lower third of the income brackets in Canada, who cannot possibly look forward to having anywhere to live if they are to depend on the legislation as it now stands on our statute books.
