maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
The veterans rehabilitation bill, so far as parliament is concerned, *is new legislation. The services to be provided under it have, however, been in effect since October 1, 1941, under the post discharge re-

Veterans Affairs
establishment order, which was approved by order in council under the authority of the War Measures Act.
The bill now before the committee has been recommended by the special committee on veterans affairs, whose recommendation, with the draft bill annexed, appears in Votes and Proceedings of this house under date of December 4.
The post discharge reestablishment order, originally adopted in 1941, was substantially revised by P.C. 5210 of July 13, 1944, and its terms have been widely publicized. It is probably the best known of all the country's rehabilitation measures. It is under this order that the Department of Veterans Affairs is authorized to assist former members of the forces in the matter of vocational training and interrupted education.
The order permits the payment of allowances, graduated in proportion to family needs, to veterans, both men and women, under the following five condition:
1.	That the veteran is willing and able to work, and has been unable to find suitable employment.
2.	That the veteran is unemployed through temporary physical incapacity.
3.	That the veteran has entered upon a business, farming or professional undertaking under his own proprietorship, and requires money for his subsistence while awaiting a first crop, or a living return from the enterprise.
4.	That the veteran has been awarded a vocational training course for the purpose of assisting him to obtain employment, or better employment.
5.	That the veteran has been awarded an educational course of university or professional . grade, either in the under-graduate or postgraduate field, or, by a comparatively recent addition to the order, for the purpose of qualifying for admission to a university.
In the case of training and educational benefits, the cost of tuition is also borne as a public expense.
There is a sixth provision giving the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act to veterans who enter insured employment. For the purpose of calculating unemployment benefit, time spent in military service is counted as if it had been spent in insured employment. In order to make this practicable the government pays into the insurance fund the contributions that would have been made during the time of the veteran's military service.
The post-discharge reestablishment order has been, and must continue to be, the backbone of the whole rehabilitation programme. Although all veterans may not have occasion to claim assistance under this legislation, its benefits are available to all. When originally adopted the order in council offered assistance, far beyond anything ever attempted in the past, for the purpose of promoting the civil reestablishment of a country's demobilized fighting forces.
Other countries have followed Canada's lead, and Canada has greatly broadened the terms of her own legislation. Close comparison with measures adopted in other countries is not possible, because each country has attuned its measures to its own local conditions. Nevertheless, I believe Canada can take pride in the fact that in this field her legislation is unsurpassed by that of any other country in breadth, scope and flexibility. For this very reason, because we were breaking new ground, and it was recognized that changes and modifications would probably be dictated by experience, it was considered advisable that the measure should be initiated by order in council. Subsequent developments have justified that decision.
The original order in council has been amended and broadened repeatedly, in order that we might keep abreast of developments and meet unforeseen difficulties as they arose. I have always considered however that so important a measure should have the sanction and authority of parliament, and I have, on a number of occasions, announced my intention at the appropriate time of asking parliament to convert this order in council into a statute. That step is now being taken. It has been taken in accordance with the procedure authorized by this house earlier in the session, when it appointed the special committee on veterans affairs to review all veterans' legislation, and recommend such action to the house as might be found appropriate.
The bill now before us differs from others which have already been dealt with, in that it is not an amending bill, but will lead to the enactment of a new statute. For the reasons already indicated, the bill has been designed to preserve the flexibility, so that unforeseen problems may be met promptly and effectively. The bill confers authority upon the government to pay allowances to veterans under clearly defined conditions.
With respect to members of Canada's armed forces, the bill contains no important additional benefits beyond those contained in the order in council. There is, however, one important new substantive provision permitting the unemployment insurance benefit to be extended to veterans of the armed forces of allied nations, under certain conditions:
Veterans Affairs

1.	That the veteran was domiciled in Canada before the war; and
2.	That the nation, in whose forces the veteran served, undertakes to make the same contribution to the unemployment insurance fund as that which the government of Canada makes with respect to our own veterans who enter insured employment.
As with most of our legislation, the order in council and the bill permit the benefits of the act to be conferred upon veterans of prewar Canadian domicile who served in the forces of His Majesty, other than Canadian forces.
The bill contains one or two minor provisions not heretofore found in the post discharge reestablishment order. For instance, wide discretion is conferred upon the minister in the matter of extending the time limits for training, in the case of disability pensioners. Experience has shown that the need for retraining of disabled veterans frequently arises long after discharge. The department has had this power for many years under its treatment regulations, but with the enactment of legislation on the subject of training it seems desirable that this provision should be brought under the Veterans Rehabilitation Act.
Another new provision allows correspondence courses to be given to patients still in hospital, without sacrifice of their subsequent training rights.
The select committee reviewed the draft legislation with meticulous care and, as with former bills, was able to render valuable assistance in redrafting some of the clauses so as to give greater protection to the veterans for whom the legislation is designed. The rates of allowances are not dealt with in the bill. These are left in the hands of the government, under the customary powers of ' regulation, in order that adjustments required by changed economic conditions in the country may be made without undue delay.
The adoption of this bill by parliament will necessarily lead to the drafting of a new order in council containing regulations pursuant to the act. The post-discharge reestablishment order, as it stands to-day, contains a great deal of subject matter which is now being transferred to an act of parliament. The new order in council will consist of the regulations which the bill authorizes the government to make.
No substantive changes in the existing regulations are contemplated at this time, but the department will always be prepared to recommend such changes, consistent with the terms of the act, as progressive developments may require in the interests of ex-service personnel.

maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in keeping with the desire of the committee, it is not my intention to make any extended remarks on this bill. The minister has already given a resume of the measure which we shall study later section by section. As one of the members of the veterans committee, I wish at this time to express my appreciation of the warm praise the minister has given the committee on various occasions. He has said it was one of the hardest working committees of the house. I think he might very well have said it was the hardest working committee, during this session.
It is also pointed out that this is a new bill rather than an amendment to an old act. It puts in statute forms the post-discharge rehabilitation orders in council that have been passed.
The bill had the general approval of the committee, not because the committee felt it was an end in itself but because the committee thought that the bill would assist toward the great end they had in view, the rehabilitation of our men who have returned from overseas. Our experience for the past twenty-five years, as the committee knows, has taught us that most veteran legislation is subject to change. We have worked more or less on a trial and error basis. I have no doubt that many changes will be necessary in the bill which is before us this afternoon. It was agreed in the committee, not only with respect to this bill but with respect to other legislation affecting veterans, that if amendments were necessary later they could be made in future meetings of the veterans' committee.
The act is to be entitled the Veterans' Rehabilitation Act. We had very little time to discuss the title in committee; as a matter of fact it was decided on only in the last moments of the last meeting of the committee. Frankly I think it can hardly be called the Veterans' Rehabilitation Act; I think it could better be called the veterans' rehabilitation assistance act, for that is really what it is. Upon looking up the definition of "rehabilitate" I found that it means to restore to former status, capacity, right, rank or privilege. This bill only assists in doing that.
The word "rehabilitation" I think has a deeper meaning for everyone. It represents the hopes and ambitions of the 750,000 to 1,000,000 men of our different services who have returned from overseas. It represents the personal and social readjustment of those people. It represents to the people of Canada and to their elected representatives their bounden duty to assure to these men who

Veterans Affairs
fought for their country that they will be properly rehabilitated and restored into the civil life of this Dominion of Canada.
There are certain things which are particularly necessary for rehabilitation, and they have been, mentioned in this committee on previous occasions. First and foremost, if we are to rehabilitate our soldiers they must have jobs. That is something about which I think we are all agreed. The soldier must have a job which is suitable to his peculiar talents and which affords him. an opportunity to better himself as time goes on. Next, the man who has returned must have a home in decent surroundings where he can educate his children and bring them up to be good citizens of this country. The. third requirement of rehabilitation to my mind is that the soldier's mind must be free from worry. He must have reached the stage where he feels he is once more a citizen of this country rather than an alien among a hostile crowd of civilians.
Taking into consideration these three things ' -jobs, homes and minds free from worry- what is the condition of the men who have returned to Canada? What do they find *when they disembark from the boats at Halifax or New York, or when they return to Montreal, Winnipeg or wherever their homes may be? These men find that from one end of Canada to the other jobs are scarce, there are no opportunities for the reemployment of our men, there are thousands of them walking the streets, there are strikes all across the country. These men find that the prospects of reemployment are less bright to-day than they have been in quite a number of years. They find that there are 36,500 returned men who are without work at this time.
This morning when the hon. member for Mackenzie was dealing with the question of housing he quoted newspaper advertisements inserted by returned service personnel who were looking for a place to live. An address was given over the radio by Mr. Woods, deputy minister of veterans' affairs, requesting the people of Canada to open up their homes to returned men. It was an eloquent appeal, and I hope it is one which will be taken to heart and acted upon by the people of this country.
This afternoon the minister stated that this bill will provide out-of-work benefits, and I think it does so in a fairly generous manner. But the young men who have returned from overseas are not looking for out-of-work benefits, they are looking for work. They do
not want to come under the Unemployment Insurance Act or under this legislation. This country cannot be built up by paying unemployment insurance or out-of-work benefits.
This bill provides for the man who has taken up business. If such a man is getting no return from his business for a period of twelve months he can obtain benefits under the act. While this may be and is very necessary, this country is not going to be built up if men have to sit back in their businesses waiting for returns for a year or possibly longer. These men would like to see the wheels of industry turning so that they can get goods on their shelves. A man who has a garage or is in some other business would like to see production under way so that he can get tools and equipment to work with at once.
I repeat that this is not a rehabilitation measure; it is simply an act for the assistance of rehabilitation. The minister referred to assistance to be given to college students and men taking vocational training. This is a wise provision. I have been pleased to hear from the heads of universities in different parts of the country that returned men who have taken up university and vocational training are showing themselves to be better than average when compared with the men in civilian life. This shows the great interest our returned men are taking in rehabilitating themselves for the days to come.
The minister spoke of the flexibility of the allowances. It is wise not to set hard and fast allowances for college students or for those receiving the other benefits. We do not know what the situation will be perhaps three or six months from to-day. Before the war a young man attending college could get board for $6 or $7 a week, but I understand that today in many cases he must pay $12 to $14 per week. Some provision may have to be made by way of regulation later on to increase the benefits and allowances to be paid to men attending our universities.
What we want to-day is an opportunity for our young men to go back to work. We want our young men back on the farms; we want our young men back in the mines; we want our young men back in industry; we want our young men back in all the activities of this country. In this great young country there are many opportunities for the young men of Canada. There has been much talk about locating the returning young men in and around the great industrial centres of Canada. We are building houses for them-at least we plan to do it; we have not done it yet. What
Veterans Affairs

we need also is to develop our northern areas. A great mineral industry awaits development there. We have the only frontier which is left in the world to-day, and there are no better men to develop this frontier than those who fought along the English channel at Caen and Falaise, in France, Holland, Italy and other countries. An opportunity must be provided for these men.
We are fortunate in having to administer the act Mr. Walter Woods, the deputy minister, a man who has earned the confidence of the veterans of this country from one end to the other by his fair administration of the Veterans Allowance Act. We have also General Burns, who is director of rehabilitation. I had the pleasure and the honour of meeting General Bums overseas just a little over a year ago, and from talking with men from different parts of Canada and with those I met overseas I know that he is highly respected and honoured by the soldiers generally. I am satisfied that he will do a splendid job. But it is not the men at the head that we have had difficulty with in administering acts for the benefit of the soldiers. It has been the underlings, if I may call them so, from one end of Canada to the other. I hope that General Bums and Walter Woods will inspire these men with the same sense of fairness as that by which they themselves are animated, so that we shall not have the criticism of this act that we have had of other veterans legislation.
I repeat that this measure does not provide for rehabilitation but for assistance in rehabilitation, and the more money we have to spend on out-of-work benefits while a man is awaiting returns from business under this act, the less in adverse ratio shall we have contributed to the rehabilitation of our young men.

maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was a member of the committee in which the bill and the regulations were gone over, and I think the committee did as good a job as possible in the time at their disposal. There is no doubt that when the committee sits again, as we all hope it will next session, the experience gained in administering the act in the interval will enable us perhaps to open it up again and make the necessary adjustments.
This bill of course is not all-inclusive so far as the veterans' welfare is concerned. It is merely a bill to provide, for the time being, assistance, both financial and in the educational field, in the reestablishment of returned service personnel. We do not want to forget for a moment that it is a temporary measure, to assist the veteran in the transition period

from war to peace. We must not make the mistake of thinking that by passing this legislation we have provided wholly for the veterans; for unless the entire economy of the country is healthy the veteran will suffer with the rest of our population in an economy that does not provide for all our people.
The bill itself is clear. There can be no mistaking the intention of those who drafted it. But the test of any legislation is in its administration. We realize that fault can be found with the administrative machinery that is set up across the country. I think the department in Ottawa is doing a fairly reasonable job, but the machinery across the country is new and' is just getting under way, with personnel being trained and all the rest of it, and there is considerable room for improvement.
There is one thought in particular that I would leave with the minister. I have met those who are working in the field on veterans affairs, in connection with vocational training, vocational guidance, and so forth, and I must say that those I have met are of a very high type with exceptional qualifications and with adequate training for the job. But the salaries paid to the office staff are very low and leave much to be desired. I have talked to several men in the offices whom I knew personally. They are capable men whom the minister would find it very difficult to replace. I know one married man with eight children who is receiving a salary of only $156 a month, yet he is working at least fourteen hours a day. When he is through at the office for the day he interviews a line-up of young veterans calling upon him at his home. So he is continuously on the job. He provides his own transportation, and he has to get around quite a bit. I do not see how you can hold that type of person on the kind of salary he is getting. There is room for an adjustment of salaries all along the line for the type of person you are getting to-day and the importance of the work they have to handle. The staffs are short-handed too. They have not enough personnel, as is quite apparent.
The members of our group were fairly well represented on the committee. The bill has been gone into thoroughly, and now we are quite willing to let it go through on the understanding, first, that there should be an adjustment in the salaries of those who are assisting in administering the act, and as well an improvement in the administrative machinery right along the line; and second, that we do not make the mistake of thinking we are settling with the veterans permanently by this legislation. It is only temporary, and our

Veterans Affairs
whole economy needs to be restored before the veteran can fit into it and make his maximum contribution to the welfare of the country.

maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
In discussing the 'bill which is now before the house may I point out that we have always in the past said that we have the best veterans legislation in the world. When you speak of something that is better than something else, it is well to look closely at the comparison that is being made.
As previous speakers have already indicated, this legislation deals with the interim period, just as the country is going through an interim stage. This legislation, while a benefit, is not intended to be a substitute for a job. It was never intended for that. But it has some advantages at this particular time, and I should like to make a few comparisons for the benefit of the committee. Perhaps the best comparison would be with our neighbours to the south.
Let me compare what we call in this country a gratuity with what the Americans call mustering-out pay. Our gratuity for a private after two years' service in Canada is S611 for a single man and $711 for a married man; in the United States the private receives $300.
As to the matter of preference in civil service jobs, in Canada the soldier with overseas service gets the preference. That amounts to a monopoly of jobs. In the United States they have a preference, and also a qualified preference. This may be something we shall have to consider later.
Out-of-work benefits in Canada amount to $50 a month and it has been recommended that the amount should be increased to $60. In the United States it is $20 a week; but when it is applied to a man and one child the Canadian benefits immediately rise above those of the United States. So far as educational and vocational training benefits are concerned, both in Canada and the United States they are of the widest eligibility; but the subsistence allowance in Canada is higher than it is in the United States. The disability pension for 100 per cent disability in the United States is $115 a month; in Canada it is based on rank and dependents and it is higher than in the United States.
These are just a few observations and a few figures which I wanted the committee to have, mainly for the purpose of pointing out that both the minister and the officials have a flexible mind on this problem; they have been not only ready but eager to make changes to meet the wishes of the committee, and I think that that augurs well for the future of veteran legislation.

maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
I was not privileged to be a member of the special committee dealing with veterans affairs, but our group had three members on the committee, and I think they contributed their fair share to the discussions. We have had reports from time to time and have read many of the discussions. I believe there is no need for our taking up any time now. I believe the committee has done good work as far as it has gone, but we hope that in the near future, as soon as the new session opens, we shall again have an opportunity to go into these matters when there will be more time, and perhaps we shall have further suggestions to make.
I realize, and it has been pointed out already, that very good legislation can be nullified to a large extent by poor administration. Under a new head, under the guidance of a man who has the interests of the veterans at heart, we may reasonably hope for satisfactory results. I believe that under the old administration some of the staff were not giving 100 per cent satisfaction. I trust the minister will see to it that their record is improved to the utmost in the interests of the veterans rather than that of the public treasury.

maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
This bill is one of a series which in the speech from the throne was foreshadowed as the "veterans' charter". When I first addressed this house I ventured to point out that legislation is only one-half of the duty of this government, and that an equally important half of its duty is to use its executive power to carry out the intent of the legislation passed by parliament so that the benefits of the measures we pass shall go actually to the people. It is to that aspect of the matter that I wish to address myself to-day, and particularly, to the serious situation in Vancouver with regard to unemployment.
The facts of that situation are these. On November 23-using round figures, and quoting the reports of the Department of Labour- there were 13,500 applicants for jobs and 4,000 vacancies, leaving 9,500 job seekers for whom there was no job existing. Of that 9,500-again by official figures-4,700 were veterans of this or the last war. The situation in Vancouver is more serious than in any other part of the country if you compare the figures for the various districts-more serious for the percentage of unemployed, and also for the small number of jobs available.
There is one impression I want to correct in the minds of hon. members. It has been said quite often in the press recently, and I should not be at all surprised if it has been

Veterans Affairs

said in this chamber, that there is a great deal of work in the woods for those who want to go to it. I have taken the trouble to look into that situation as it affects Vancouver and British Columbia, and I find that very recently -within the last two weeks-there were only eighty-five jobs open in logging and lumbering for people in the Pacific districts, and on another day there were about 103 jobs open in those pursuits. That compares very ill with the 9,500 out of work, and I think it conclusively shows, Mr. Chairman, that the suggestion that men are not willing to go to work in the woods does not apply in British Columbia. There may be many jobs open in the future, when skilled men are found for special jobs which allow the opening of other camps and mines, but at the present time these jobs are in the potential stage only and do not actually exist. I understand that the great field for jobs in the woods at the present time is in northern Ontario and not in British Columbia.
Now, let us not be under the impression that in the spring when these key men are found there will be thousands and thousands of jobs in British Columbia. I have a newspaper clipping here, quoting a reliable source close to the logging industry, that it is anticipated that in the spring there will be 1,500 jobs opening up in the woods, and roughly, the situation in Vancouver is, I repeat, that 4,700 veterans at present are out of work.

maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext: What is the source of the hon. member's estimate of 1,500 jobs?

maintopic: ALLOWANCES FOR TEMPORARILY UNEMPLOYED- VOCATIONAL OR EDUCATIONAL TRAINING- UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
The source is a newspaper clipping, a reporter of a Vancouver paper talking to someone engaged in the logging industry. I hope, with the minister, that it will be many more than 1,500, but I simply throw that out as a warning.
Turning for a moment to the question of housing in Vancouver, we find the same deplorable position. A recent statement issued by the emergency shelter authority shows 4,143 persons listed on the books of the administration as having no or unsuitable housing, and of that number, 3,483, or more than three-fourths, are ex-servicemen. In the month of November there were 833 placements only.
Another significant thing about these figures is that, of those placements, 450 couples were couples of whom the husband enlisted in Vancouver or in British Columbia, and in the case of 237 couples the veteran had come from some other part of Canada and is now trying to settle in Vancouver. So that there again

we find that the benefits we hope to put on the statute books are not now getting over to the veterans.
I want to say something very briefly about the causes of this situation. We all know that out in British Columbia we have the most wonderful climate in Canada, and that it attracts people from all over the country. That, of course, is actual fact, but as a result, as I will show, we have very many more people in the province than we had before the war. But offsetting that, our industry is pretty well primary industry-lumbering, mining and fishing-and the openings for employment, particularly in Vancouver, are probably not as extensive as they are in the big cities of the east. Again, with respect to seasonal work in our mines and logging camps, there is always a shut-down around Christmas time, and that is contributing to the situation as well. Of course, we have a shortage of key men; but, as I have pointed out, this business about people being unwilling to go to the woods does not apply in Vancouver, where only 103 jobs are open. Other things have contributed to the difficulty at the present time. In the first place, it is estimated that forty per cent more than the number who enlisted are taking their discharge from Vancouver barracks, that the total being discharged from the armed forces at. the present time is 2,500 a month or more -I believe it was 3,500 in November-and that there was a war-time influx into our war industries, shipbuilding and aeroplane building, which have completely shut down now, of some 90,000 from the prairie provinces. That figure is an estimate, and it may be a little too high. But in addition, the figures I have from newspapers show that there are about 300 people coming into Vancouver every month from the prairies or from the east; they are all closing in on that city looking for jobs, and the "job base," if I may put it that way, is one of the narrowest in all Canada.
I should not want to have it thought that the citizens of Vancouver are doing nothing to cure the situation, because as a matter of fact they are doing a great deal. They started a citizens' committee and a caimpaign "Invest in the Veteran." They set out in the hope of being able to get each one of the 2,500 businesses and industries in and around the city to take on at least one veteran, and larger enterprises to take on many more indeed. Tfiat is of course the best possible way in which a situation such as this can be solved, because it is upon private industry that we depend almost entirely for employment in this country. I want to call attention to the efforts of the citizens' committee, because it is a

Veterans Affairs
very creditable move indeed and it is the way in which the problem of unemployment in the final analysis can be solved in every part of the country-the only way. But while I say that private industry is the body which gives employment in this country, I do not relieve the government from responsibility in this connection. Although private industries are the actors on the stage, the stage setting which enables the actors to carry their play through successfully is the responsibility of the government, and there are many ways in which the government can assist in that stage setting which as yet I have not seen them undertake. One of these ways is this present bill, but that is not enough by any means.
I suggest that there is not a sufficient lead from the government in this connection, and there has not been in the government's policy sufficient flexibility to deal with a situation in a particular locality in Canada, even though the general over-all picture may not be nearly as bad as the local situation. I would ask the government now to give that lead and to provide that flexibility. With this in mind, so that it will not be thought that I am talking vaguely and in generalities, I have specific suggestions which I wish to make to each of seven or eight ministers of the crown. Since they are not all in their seats at the moment I will address these suggestions to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, whose job it is of course-it must be his principal job- to coordinate all activities of the government which can be of benefit to veterans.
We have had from the Minister of Reconstruction the statement that there is to be no public works programme to relieve the situation in Vancouver, although that has been asked for. I have no particular objection myself to no public works programme, chiefly because I am quite sure that it would take so long to get it actually started that the situation must be met by more expeditious means. I do not think the government is right in withholding public works generally at the present time. The shelf project is all very well; but it might also be a very good idea not to cultivate the squirrel habit when you put things on your shelves. If these public works were prepared they could be used to advantage in Vancouver to-day. However, let us assume that we shall not have public works, since that has been definitely stated by a minister.
Then we have the Minister of National Defence, who is responsible for dischare policy in the armed forces. We have had it from the minister that people may be discharged in whatever part of Canada they may wish. Again in general I have no particular objection to 47696-2081
that but I do object, when an emergency situation such as this arises, when everyone is crying in Vancouver for work, that no change is made in that policy at the present time. It is ridiculous that the government should go on discharging in Vancouver people who did not enlist there, knowing that there are no jobs to be found at the moment and that as soon as they have used up their month's pay and started on their reestablishment gratuities they will be back on the labour market, using their credits for living expenses, which I am sure was never the intention of the government, and certainly not the intention of parliament. This is definitely the time when the discharge policy should be reviewed with the object of stopping temporarily the discharge of service personnel in Vancouver if they did not enlist there or if they have not a definite job to go to.
Let us combine that question of the discharge of men with the Department of Reconstruction on the matter of housing. I have given the housing situation in Vancouver. It is very serious indeed. Over 3,400 veterans are improperly housed. If we are to go on discharging men in Vancouver at the rate of 140 per cent of enlistments, I suggest that the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Reconstruction could well get together and give Vancouver a greater priority for housing materials for veterans, thereby getting these people under cover and providing a greater chance of employment.
I turn now to the Department of Labour, By all means, let us stop this influx of 300 a month from the prairies. Let us advertise in the papers on the prairies and bring the full weight of the Department of Labour to bear in order to show men that it is useless to go there now and add to the unemployment situation. Let us tell them that if they go out they will be doing the veterans who are at present in Vancouver, a bad turn by competing with them for the few available jobs. Let us impress upon people the unwisdom of going out to Vancouver at the present time. People will respond to that kind of thing. They are not fools, and if they get sound advice from someone they respect I am sure the Canadian people will follow it.
I wish to commend the Department of Labour for having agreed to pay the fares of those moving out of Vancouver who are going to jobs in some other part of the country. It is a thoroughly commendable step to take, and it is one of the things that each department of the government should be thinking of, because all these little nickels that each minister can throw in, if I may call them that, will make a dollar by the time the whole cabinet has put
Veterans Affairs

in its contribution, and will go a long way towards solving the problem, that we are now discussing.
May I now turn to the Department of Mines and Resources and to the Department of Fisheries. There is much work to be done in the future in each of these departments. Perhaps the dominion-provincial conference is holding up progress at the moment because no agreement has been reached. But when an agreement is reached between the dominion and the provinces there will be a tremendous expansion of the work of reforestation and the propagation of fish. There will be a large field for trained foresters, hatchery men and the like. Hon. members are aware of the fact that we are short of trained men in these fields. We have large numbers of veterans, the best men you could possibly get, who have been outside and living that kind of life for four or five years. They are ideal men for these jobs. They could1 be taken in hand and put in training schools so that when an agreement is reached between the dominion and the provinces that work would not be further held up for lack of trained men.
Another job which could be done immediately, particularly in Vancouver, comes under the Postmaster General. We have not yet got back to double delivery of mail in Vancouver. Air mail which comes in in the morning is actually held over until the following day because of the lack of afternoon deliveries. I have had several resolutions from various bodies in Vancouver. One of them came from the citizens' rehabilitation council, which deals with veterans. It urged that a second delivery be inaugurated. I have made reference to the committee of citizens in Vancouver which is sponsoring this campaign for jobs for veterans. Is this government going to lag behind in these matters? Where there is useful work to be done in the whole community, does the government intend to leave until next spring or some time in the future the employment of additional men on the postal routes? It will not be as valuable then as it would be now, because in addition to taking several hundred of these veterans off the out-of-work rolls in Vancouver it would give inspiration to the committee there. They would know that the federal government is taking an active part in the citizens' campaign which is making such a great effort to help to employ more men. I suggest to the Minister of Veterans Affairs that this matter be taken up with the Postmaster General-not next week, not after Christmas, but now; and that instructions be sent out, to-day if possible, that these men be taken on the postal staff and that a second delivery be instituted at once.. This

is not a matter of relief; this is not employment for employment's sake; it is a necessary job and it should and must be done right now.
I now come to the Department of Finance. There is much that they can do. They can throw in their nickel's worth too. I have two principal suggestions to make here. My first one is decentralization. At the present time prices are fixed in Ottawa. Hon. members are aware that because Ottawa is three thousand miles away the people here do not fully know the conditions on the coast. They know only what they are told by their branch offices out there. In actual practice it has been found that it takes two months to get a price fixed for a new commodity. Think of what that has done to the reestablishment of civilian trade. Think of what it has done to the Christmas trade; think of what it has contributed to the present unemployment situation in Vancouver. There should be decentralization now; there should be some flexibility in this price fixing. If the people on the spot were given at least some measure of price fixation, within certain limits laid down in Ottawa, they would be able to do the job perfectly well and still prevent inflation, and at the same time get things moving.
Recently in this house we heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare say that his family allowances could not operate unless they were decentralized. He has only seven employees in Ottawa, and that is the kind of thing I suggest should be considered by the Minister of Finance at once in the hope of getting some speed in this matter.
The second principle that I suggest the Minister of Finance should look into is that of flexibility. I can give 'the committee an illustration which will show what I mean. At the present time there is a shortage of lath in the building trades. I have it from sources in Vancouver that mills are cutting up wood for firewood instead of making it into lath because under the vagaries of the wartime prices and trade board they get more for wood than they do for lath. If that is so, does it not show that there is need for someone from the wartime prices and trade board being on the spot in these various centres, someone who will go round, ferret things out and correct these maladjustments which are holding back reconstruction?
I know this, from having been told by an officer of the wartime prices and trade board, that during the war that body worked on the principle that if the fixing of prices forced a

Veterans Affairs
man out of business they did not mind. That was all right during the war because there was an inexhaustible demand for labour in war industry, and if someone was forced out of an inessential trade he could get a job at once in a war industry. Now the circumstances are entirely different. You cannot afford, by your price control mechanism, to force anyone out of business, and you cannot afford to force him out of essential lines into other and less essential lines. Decentralization would tend to greater flexibility and provide more jobs.
Everyone in the house knows that deflation is one of the causes of unemployment. In our attempts to prevent inflation do not let us go to the other extreme and deflate and cause unemployment. 'Let us look at the situation and see whether in fact there are elements of deflation in the activities of the wartime prices and trade board. I know that everyone in the house is for price control, but it must be borne in mind that we have taken away the price incentive to do business. If we are to undertake to control the economy of the country in this way, then we must not do only half a job. We must do the other half by providing some incentive other than the price incentive to keep business going and to keep on expanding. I suggest that that must be looked into very carefully by the Department of Finance, particularly in relation to the situation in Vancouver.
Finally, I come to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I suggest that his function is to coordinate the activities of all these other ministries, to hold out the bag so that they can put their nickels in and by that means get something done in connection with this matter. "Get cracking!" Finally, I urge upon the minister with all my strength that he should go out to Vancouver-

He should talk to that citizens' committee and find out what the government can do to assist them; he should talk to the veterans and find out what their troubles are. And, having made that personal inspection, having talked to the people, he will come back here with many more ideas than I have been able to give him this afternoon-and I believe I have given him a few.
The most effective way in which problems such as those existing in Vancouver can be solved is by a minister of the crown making an investigation and, while he is doing so,
getting behind the local movement and giving it the greatest possible boost. Let him show the employers that this civic effort is not some crazy man's idea but a great national effort to which all can contribute on behalf of the veterans.
The limit to which the government can go, in my view, was set out by Mr. Churchill at the time V-2 bombs were falling. He was asked what he was doing to stop them, and he answered in this way:	"I was inspecting the
damage done by one of the bombs the other day, when a man who lived in one of those houses came up to me and said, 'What are you doing to stop these things?' I answered him by saying, 'I am doing everything humanly possible'." This, I suggest, is the only limit this government can accept in a situation such as that which confronts the veterans this winter. When the government has done everything humanly possible, it has done enough. I do say, however, that at this time, and certainly in connection with the situation in Vancouver, very little has been done. Certainly not enough has been done, and that which has been done has not been sufficiently publicized out on the Pacific coast. At the present time the people out there are angry because veterans are unemployed. But, as I said when I first came to the house, they are just as angry because they do not seem to get any response from Ottawa when they attempt to lay their difficulties before the government.

I appreciate, as he does, the situation in which returning men find themselves,, and I understand that in Vancouver the situation is probably worse than it is in any other part of Canada. But when any hon. member suggests that appeals should be made by one part of the country to another asking that people stay out of certain fields of employment so that veterans may be employed, I suggest that such procedure would not be for the welfare of the country as a whole. If the unemployed people in the prairie provinces,, about whom he spoke, were to take his advice and stay home rather than go to Vancouver to seek employment, I do not know what they would do. Surely that is not a solution of the problem. I should expect the hon. member to have greater vision than that. Temporary
Veterans Affairs

relief of unemployment in Vancouver certainly will not take care of the unemployment problem across Canada. I have no doubt the suggestion was made in the veterans committee that these returned men should be cared for and kept on full pay and allowances until such time as they might be properly rehabilitated. I should think that would be much more to the point than the suggestion that unemployed people in the prairie provinces should not go in search of employment, to Vancouver or anywhere else.
