maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: This bill, of which the second reading has just been endorsed by the house, is a bill to amend the Veterans' Land Act. Like the bill amending the War Service Grants Act, with which we have already dealt, this bill has been recommended to the house by the select committee on veterans affairs.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Unanimously?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes. The committee's recommendation, which includes the draft bill, was presented on Monday, November 26, and appears in the Votes and Proceedings of that day. The act which it is proposed to amend was adopted in 1942, also upon recommendations of a committee of this house.
The amendments now offered represent for the most part orders in council adopted under the War Measures Act arising out of administrative experience and designed to increase the scope of settlement opportunities.
With the end of the war it has been deemed desirable that the legislation should be reviewed by a select committee of this house and that amendments having their sanction in orders in council should be embodied in the statute with the full authority of parliament. The select committee was also authorized by this house to consider the whole field of veterans' legislation and was invited to suggest additional amendments which might be deemed appropriate. These instructions the select committee has acted upon.
The bill now before us includes not only those provisions which had already been adopted by order in council but two or three additional clauses. The bill as recommended by the committee has been accepted by the government and is before the house in the form of a government bill.
Aside from orders in council, the two principal amendments recommended by the select committee are: first, a more precise definition of the service qualifications required of applicants for settlement under the act; second, a specific assertion that the acceptance of the benefits conferred by the act shall not dis-
Veterans Land Act

qualify a veteran from taking his seat in parliament. With respect to the definition of service, it has been decided to follow the very carefully considered language of the War Service Grants Act. The desirability of the second new provision arises from the fact that numbers of members of the forces were members of parliament or have been elected to parliament. It did not seem in the public interest that veterans should be deprived of their reestablishment rights by reason of the fact that the people of Canada had chosen them to be their representatives in parliament. The other amendments, with one exception to which I shall refer, are those which had been adopted by order in council as the result of administrative experience.
One group of such amendments increases the ceiling prices for contracts of settlement. The original act, as passed in 1942, provided that the maximum cost of an individual settlement should not exceed $4,800. It was found that the administration could not acquire a sufficient number of satisfactory farms and suitable small holdings within that maximum. The new ceiling which has been in effect for some time is $6,000. Needless to say, there are some areas of very high quality land where farms and settlements cannot be acquired even at this price. However, by actual experience the director has been able to acquire close to five hundred thousand acres of farm land suitable for settlement within the ceiling now prescribed and, in addition, approximately twenty thousand acres of carefully selected sites for small holdings. The provision regarding ceilings recommended to the house by the select committee is, in form and substance, identical with the powers which the director has already enjoyed for some time under a series of orders in council.
The other major subject covered by this amending bill is the provision for enabling settlement to take place on provincial crown lands, upon Indian lands, and upon land within national parks or otherwise vested in the crown in right of the dominion.
To understand the history of these amendments, it is desirable that we bear in mind the fundamental purpose of the Veterans' Land Act. That purpose is the reestablishment of veterans, in this case the reestablishment of veterans with farming experience or a farming background, in farm homes, or upon small holdings where the cultivation of the soil contributes jointly with some other occupation to the maintenance of the veteran and his family. In order that this statement may not be incomplete, I should mention that commercial fishing is dealt with on a parity with farming. The important point in this con-
text is, however, that our dominion legislation in this field is aimed specifically at the reestablishment of veterans on the land under conditions which offer reasonable assurances of success to the average industrious practical settler.
The Veterans' Land Act contemplates a loan and, under certain conditions, a free grant of a certain proportion of the value of the enterprise.
It was considered essential-and this was repeatedly emphasized by members from all parts of the house-when the act was under debate in 1942, that each individual settlement project should be carefully scrutinized from the point of view of both the qualifications of the veteran and the suitability of the land.
Provincial governments are also interested in settlement from the point of view of the opening up of new and unsettled lands in frontier areas. Representations were received from several of the provinces urging that the Veterans' Land Act should be modified so as to be of assistance in this regard.
There is, of course, nothing in the act to prevent settlement upon crown land where, in the judgment of the director and his advisory committees, the project offers reasonable assurance of success. It is well known, however, that a great deal of provincial crown land is wild land outside the settled areas, and that the man who undertakes to bring a tract of wild land under cultivation faces a certain element of risk. In practical experience we find very little such land that constitutes in its present condition adequate security for a loan such as is contemplated under the standard provisions of the Veterans' Land Act.
While the dominion and the provinces, for the reasons indicated,, necessarily approached this whole subject from quite different directions, we considered that there need be no irreconcilable difficulty about combining the two purposes.
The legislation was designedly drafted in flexible form, because the proposals of the several provinces differed greatly from each other.
The contribution to settlement, which the dominion is prepared to make under these agreements, is a dircet grant not exceeding the maximum free grant, which accompanies a standard settlement contract on a developed farm.
The amount is $2,320, and the act requires that this sum shall be used for one or more of a variety of purposes set forth with great clarity in the section of the bill which is now being introduced. It is open to the provinces

Veterans Land Act
to make some additional contribution to the settler's success, and several provinces have indicated their intention of doing so.
The order in council, which it is now proposed to incorporate in the act, has been at least partly justified by experience. Three provinces have already entered into agreements with the dominion and negotiations with three others are in an advanced stage.
The result is that the substantial number of Canadian veterans who were reared on our northern frontiers can, if they wish to do so, return to that part of the country whose ways and resources they know and understand. They can return to the frontiers and receive a substantial measure of state assistance under terms that are broad enough to permit them to undertake careers in which farming, fishing, forestry, trapping or a combination of several of these typical Canadian occupations, may contribute to their livelihoods.
An almost exactly similar provision was adopted with respect to Indian veterans who wish to settle upon Indian lands. Such lands cannot be given as security for a loan, but the Minister of Veterans Affairs is authorized to enter into an agreement with the Minister of Mines and Resources for the purpose of ensuring that members of our Indian bands, who have served nobly in the war, shall not be denied assistance in settlement upon lands within Indian reserves.
While these clauses were under consideration by the select committee, another problem arose which was dealt with in the same way. Numbers of members of our armed forces were born and brought up in such towns as Banff and Jasper, which are situated within national parks. It is dominion government-policy that such lands may not be alienated, and cases arose where residents of park lands were unable to enjoy the benefits of the Veterans' Land Act by reason of this fact.
Accordingly the select committee has recommended-and the government has accepted the proposal-that the Minister of Veterans Affairs -shall be authorized to enter into an agreement with the Minister of Mines and Resources providing for settlement on park lands or, indeed, any other crown lands for which the Minister of Mines and Resources is responsible.
I am advised that the provision is broad enough, for instance, to cover settlement in the Northwest Territories, if such a case should .arise.
In submitting this bill to the committee, I think we should endorse without the slightest hesitation the recommendations of the very able committee of this house who gave their fine consideration to the measure.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The committee agreed to recommend this measure unanimously, in so far as it now stands, with certain reservations, on the understanding that at the next-session the committee could be reconvened and then offer any further amendments that might be necessary to take care of provisions not now contained in the bill. As pointed out, a committee of sixty ex-servicemen gave lengthy and detailed study to the matter, under the able chairmanship of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the discussions were at all times non-partisan.
The original Veterans' Land Act was set up, as the minister has stated, after a careful study by a special committee of the house in July, 1942. The preamble made it clear that the proposed measure did not restrict its terms to full-time agriculture, and although the principal objective was for full-time agricultural settlement, a veteran might secure a holding and be assisted in settlement even though he had other employment.
The total expenditure per settler was at that time $4,800, of which $1,200 might be for stock and equipment; section 13 has been amended to provide a maximum of $6,000, the rate of interest being three and a half per cent; and after ten years of settlement under the contract a maximum of $2,320 of this $6,000 becomes a grant to the settler.
The bill was founded on the principle that the veteran should have a substantial equity in the land. Mortgage companies used to contend that a farmer should have a fifty per cent equity in his land in order to be assured of success. The central mortgage bank was founded on the basis of a twenty per cent equity, and this bill provides a forty-three per cent equity, including ten per cent paid down by the veteran when he procures settlement.
Post-war farming has been considered, first, as a way of life and, second, as a business. There is a difference there because, after all, it has been considered by governments in the past that it was essential to have a number of people decentralized to settle on land. First, let us look at farming as a way of life. When it comes to business there are difficulties that crop up periodically. Great changes have taken place in agricultural production in the past few years. Mechanization has displaced many farm hands. During the war years British agriculture has become the most highly mechanized in the world. That is something different from the condition which obtained a few years ago.
There is no provision in this bill for settlers to purchase power equipment cooperatively, and $1,200 will not go far in that direction.
Veterans Land Act

That is something which I should have liked to see attended to, but I do not wish to make an issue of it at this time. We must recognize, however, that if the scheme is to be successful the principle of parity must be taken into consideration. In this connection I would quote briefly from a statement I made in July, 1942, when the act was set up. I should like to read what I said in regard to the question of parity:
May I say at the beginning that if it were not for the fact that I have some faith in the future, and a hope that agricultural parity will eventually be established in Canada, I would not have been able to support the bill even in principle. In the great nation to the south of us, the United States, there has been parity between agricultural and other products for a year now, and under the Washington wheat agreement of June 27, 1942, signed by the Argentine, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, the representatives of these nations have recognized the basis of a parity price for wheat which will return a fair remuneration to the producers as well as being fair to the consumer. On the basis of these agreements, and having regard to what has been done in the United States, I think we may hope that we are doing these settlers justice by establishing them on the land, because we hope that they will be able to carry on under parity prices, in the future at any rate. As I say, if it were not for that hope I for one could not have supported the bill.
As I said then, if it had not been for that hope I could not have supported the bill in July, 1942. I regret that the pious hope which I had at that time has not materialized effectively. During the past three and a half years we know what has happened in connection with wheat agreements, and how international conferences have fallen down in this respect. Agricultural producers in western Canada alone, as has been pointed out in other debates, are receiving, as a result of controls, approximately $255,000,000 less for this year's grain crop than they would have received on the open markets of the world, and live stock and dairy produce are on a par with grain. We have taken from one-third to fifty per cent less, while the implements of production which these settlers must purchase are on the basis of open world market prices.
According to western real estate men who appeared before the veterans committee, land values have risen twenty-five per cent since the beginning of the war. Now the ceiling price on grain is on the average a little better than twenty-five per cent over our present floor prices. You can see, therefore, the necessity of some basis of parity. No provision is made for that in the present act, should we enter into another depression, and these settlers will be caught in a deflationary set of circumstances. There is no provision to assist 
the veteran to start in business. That should have been taken care of in the rehabilitation act. If a young veteran with financial means of his own wishes to start up in business, he finds under the	controls	that	are in force
to-day, and the priorities, that he cannot procure the necessary goods without being forced into partnership with someone who is already established. This applies to men and women alike.
Section 35 was amended to facilitate the negotiation of agreements with the various provinces for the use of their provincial land to provide	for	assistance	to veterans.
These agreements provide assistance to veterans as farmers, as small holders, for forestry establishments, for commercial fishermen, for trappers and so on, with a grant up to $2,320.
As mentioned	by	the	hon.	member forRoyal, speaking	of	the	north country, I
believe that in this great dominion we are fortunate to have vast undeveloped natural resources, mining, lumber and so on, and this provision certainly assists the veterans along these lines. There are great possibilities in this respect.
With regard to administration, the director stated that some of the delay during the first years of this war had been deliberate on the part of the administration. As the committee will realize, wives must appear with the husband before the settlement committee. The committee must be assured that the wife is qualified to carry on as the husband. Many thousands of our men married overseas. Many of those men are home and their wives cannot as yet obtain passage to this country. There are many embarrassing situations, and with the present unemployment in Canada the veterans are here and the wives overseas. The men are spending their allowances of one kind and another looking for work or settlement. A small article appeared in one of the last issues of the paper from the veterans' department, carrying this heading: Wife a Burden?
A veteran applying for benefits under a section of the Veterans' Land Act which authorizes a loan at three and one-half per cent to pay off a mortgage on property already owned, was told to bring in a list of his encumbrances. He brought in his marriage certificate.
There is really a lot to that. It is an encumbrance to the poor chap under circumstances as they exist to-day. There are many thousands of such cases. While I would not urge that our men should stay overseas, I would hope that some transportation could be made available to get those wives back to this country as soon as possible. That is very important.

Veterans Land Act
The original intention of this act was for land settlement rather than small holdings. In my opinion, the efforts of the administration have been directed more to centralization of small holdings near, and in some cases, within large cities, than land settlement. We all realize that everything possible must be done to provide housing for the veterans and their dependents.
My colleague, the hon. member for Royal, made an urgent appeal to the people of Canada along that line, and I trust it will be heeded by them. The cost of constructing these houses has risen from 35 to 50 per cent since the commencement of the war. We all know how difficult it is to get houses in this country to-day. We have wartime housing, national housing and our Veterans' Land Act, and all centralized. I do not think we should follow the principle of setting up communities in this country. I know it is difficult at the present time to do otherwise because of controls. It is necessary that materials and all that kind of thing be purchased in the mass through cooperation, and therefore it is difficult to get away from controls. But I am afraid it does not augur well for the future of this country. I should like to see decentralization take place along that line as quickly as possible. Personally I am opposed to centralization of these veterans' settlements, especially when there is no assistance at present in this set-up for individuals who want to get back to the place from which they enlisted, the small village or town in the country. While provision is made to improve the present difficulty, at the present time it is almost impossible to carry out the arrangement.
I was reading some of the debates that took place in 1942 when this act was under discussion. At that time some hon. members of the government pointed out they hoped that centralization of veterans' communities would never take place in this country. It may well be that the administration of land settlement and small holdings will have to be separated in Canada, because it is most important that we provide housing for those people, and to have both phases properly carried out. It may be necessary to separate them and to set up two boards of administration.
On November 1, 1945, there were 18,705 applications for qualifications for establishment under the act either for farming or for small holdings. It is estimated that by the end of 1946 there will be over 35,000 applications in the dominion. Of these it is estimated that 17,400 will be established by the
end of 1946 as follows: 6,420 as farmers; 10,225 as small holders and 825 as commercial fishermen.
In my view this new bill is good as far as it goes. It is an excellent bill and a great improvement over the old Soldier Settlement Act. But as I have already pointed out, there are shortcomings. We wish to facilitate the passing of the measure just as quickly as possible to assist the veterans and their dependents. The veterans' committee of the house have worked hard and given of their best. We have the assurance that such a veterans' committee will be reconvened immediately after the commencement of the next session of parliament, and that further amendments covering the points I have raised will be permitted. All of us who' have been close to this situation realize that within the next two or three years new problems pertaining to the rehabilitation of our veterans and their families will be cropping up, and that members associated with that work in this parliament will be called upon to give close attention to this committee for the next two or three sessions of parliament.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
As the minister has said, this bill was reported unanimously from the veterans affairs committee. There were several reservations in the minds of hon. members, not only in the group with which I am connected but in other groups in the house, as to the sufficiency of all the sections of this bill to meet the purposes for which it was passed, namely, permanently to establish returned men in civilian life on farms. I believe that was the original purpose of the act, although, as the last speaker and the minister have said, there was another clause introduced in the act, namely, the small holdings clause which, while not displacing the main part of the act, has assumed an important place in it. Personally I think it has a place in Canada and should be encouraged.
While in some of the things I say with respect to the bill as it stands at present I may appear to be critical, I want it clearly understood that I believe that this bill is an improvement on the old Soldier Settlement Act. I had a lot to do with that act, and with the people who settled under it, and I am sure that this measure is an improvement over the old act.
I have three main objections to the bill, which I believe caused the failure of the old Soldier Settlement Act, and they have not been entirely eliminated in this bill. In the first place, under the old Soldier Settlement Act land, stock and equipment were bought at inflated prices. They were bought in 1919
Veterans Land Act

and 1920 when, as everyone knows, prices in Canada were inflated. As a result, under that act the settlers found themselves in great difficulty. In the second place the failure of the old Soldier Settlement Act was due to the fact that in settling under that act the soldier did not have sufficient equity in his land. He made a ten per cent payment and the rest of the debt was charged against him. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, no mortgage company will accept loans on that basis. No mortgage company would grant a loan of ninety per cent on the land. In most cases fifty per cent is the maximum that they will accept. In the third place I believe that the old Soldier Settlement Act failed because the soldier settling under it did not have enough capital to make a success of his business. In many cases he was operating an. uneconomic unit.
Let us see what we have done to eliminate these three main causes of the failure of the old act. When this act was drawn up in 1942-and I was on the committee along with some other members of this house who reviewed it-we made certain suggestions with respect to improvements in it. Some of them may have been accepted, but others have not. I believe that they will eventually have to be accepted before the act can be the success which we all hope it will be.
Are we settling settlers under this act at inflated prices? I believe that we should ask ourselves that question. Is the land that we are buying for the soldier settlers under this act being bought at its true value, or what may be its future value in Canada? The evidence given by real estate dealers who appeared before the committee of the house was that land prices had increased by approximately twenty-five per cent. Some who appeared before the committee were unable to express an opinion, but of those who did, that was the lowest figure at which they placed the increase in the value of land over the 1940 value.
My personal experience is that, at least in the better farming areas of Canada, there has been an increase to an extent of at least fifty per cent over farm land values which existed in 1940. Again we are settling our returned men on lands which are being sold at values considerably enhanced over those of 1940. This would be all right if we had any assurance that land would remain at those prices, or that agricultural prices would remain at their present levels. Under those circumstances land values would become stabilized at present levels.
But we have no such guarantee. As a matter of fact, the floor prices which now exist in

respect of cereals, and which have been established by the government, are at least twenty-five per cent below present prices. If we allow the prices so set to become permanent floor prices, then certainly we are faced with a deflation in farm values. Many of the soldiers who are being settled, under these circumstances, would find their equities disappear within the next few years.
For the moment let us consider stock. When the men come back they will have to buy stock. Any hon. member who has had any connection with agriculture will know that the present price of a milch cow in Canada is from $150 to $200. That is the price for any reasonably good animal. Similar animals could have been bought in 1939 or 1940 for from $75 to $100. Again, when we proceed to buy stock for these settlers, or when they spend their $1,200 for stock and equipment, they will be asked to spend it in an inflated market. While we have made some attempt to stabilize prices in Canada, and have had a certain measure of success, those prices will not remain stable unless we maintain for our agricultural products floor prices at or near present price levels, or the present selling prices of those products.
Let us now consider the second point, namely the equity the soldier will have in his land. In this respect the present measure is a great improvement over that which was found in the old soldier settlement scheme. The original act passed in 1942 set aside $3,600 for land and buildings and $1,200 for stock and equipment. The $1,200 was a grant to the soldier, provided that he retained possession of the land for ten years. He also received a rebate of 334 per cent of the $3,600. This left him an equity of about fifty-five per cent in the land and equipment under that agreement after he had made his ten per cent initial payment.
We stated at that time that we did not believe $3,600 would buy a proper unit for farming purposes in Canada. The director, and some others who appeared before the committee in 1942, seemed to think we were wrong. However, when the act was put into operation they found they could not secure land at that price, with the result that by order in council the amount for land and buildings was increased to $4,800. It was found later that even this would not buy the necessary amount of land, and another regulation was passed allowing the $1,200 granted for stock and equipment to be used for the purchase of land.
I am reasonably sure that those men who are out to-day buying land under the authorization of the Veterans' Land Act are getting

Veterans Land Act
very little more in land value for their $6,000 than was obtained in 1942 for $3,600. There has been an increase in land values to approximately that extent.
The $1,200 now being allowed in the purchase of land is not allowed by way of a grant. Rather it becomes part of the' loan, and only 334 per cent of it is written off. This makes a difference of about $920 in the equity a soldier would have in his land. It was the intention of the government, as stated at that time, to see that the soldier had a real equity in his land. I maintain that this $1,200, which can be used for the purchase of land, should be a grant, the same as it would be if he used it for the purchase of stock and equipment.
In my view, many failures which took place under the old soldier settlement scheme could be traced to the fact that the soldier did not have enough capital with which to work an economic farming unit. Surveys which have been made in Canada by various agricultural colleges as to what is required by way of capital to operate a successful farming unit show, in, almost every instance, that up to a certain amount, the more capital one has invested, the greater are his chances of successful operation. As a matter of fact, it is recognized to-day that a successful farming operation cannot be carried on without a capital investment of at least $10,000, and that there is a much greater likelihood of success if the investment is about $15,000. With the greater investment one stands a much better chance of success than with the smaller one.
Again, that greater investment gives the farmer a better chance to educate his children and to enjoy some of those amenities of life to which, in my view, the farm population are entitled, just as much as are people living in the cities and towns. To enjoy these amenities the farmer must have a capital investment sufficient to enable him to operate an economic unit. In my view $6,000 is not enough nor do I think it is enough to establish a returned man on a unit on which he would have a chance of success, or of educating his children, or of giving them the proper medical attention or of those other amenities of life to which we in Canada believe we are entitled, and which some cannot have.
I have some suggestions which I offer for the consideration of the committee. In the first place, I believe that payments under the act should be made on a parity basis. When the act was before the committee in 1942 I suggested the insertion of the following section:
In any year during which the selling price of the commodities produced _ by the veteran falls relatively to the cost price of the goods and services purchased by him as compared with the similar selling .and cost prices which prevailed during the year in which this act will have come into force-to be known as the base year-the payments due shall be reduced by an amount proportionate to the decrease in the purchasing power of the agricultural products in that year as compared with the base year.
Those payments would be considered payment in full for such year. I feel sure that, if some such section were in the act, the settlers who would come under its operation would have a much better chance of success than they have at the present time. After experience, it is my belief that, had the old soldier settlement scheme under which the settlers were placed had a section such as the one I have suggested, there would not have been constant applications to Ottawa during the years for revisions of the act for the purpose of making it possible for soldier settlers to remain on their lands. Even with all the concessions that have been granted, of over 25,000 who settled on the land only a little more than 4,000 have been able to complete their payments up to date. Unless we introduce some parity clause in the present land act we shall find ourselves again facing the same difficulty. Delegations of soldier organizations will be coming to Ottawa in five or ten years trying to get some revision made to the act. The soldier does not want charity; all he wants is justice and a fair chance in our Canadian economy. He can get that only if we have some such clause in the act.
The second thing which I believe should be done is to make more capital available to the settler. As I stated before, I believe it takes at least $19,000 to operate an economically equipped unit, and that much capital should be made available to the settler under the act. It need not necessarily be a grant; it might be a loan. With the way in which payments now operate we could increase the total loan to $10,000, so that an economical unit could be obtained by the settler. He would then be able to get sufficient stock and equipment to work it in the way in which it should be worked if it is to be a success.
The third thing which I believe should be done is to try to make more land available to the settlers. The board is having a great deal of difficulty in getting land which it wants. We were told in the committee in 1942 that in all probability there would be 100,000 applications under this act for permanent farm holdings during the first three years after the completion of the war. I believe that to date we have had some 35,000 applications for
Veterans Land Act

small and permanent holdings, but as yet we have1 settled only a small number because we have not the land available.
In certain parts of Canada large areas of land are being held by different companies. Originally this land was given to these companies as grants. Such grants were made to the railroads, to the Hudson's Bay company and to others. Some of this land is still unsettled; it is still in the raw state, but it is fairly close to railroads, schools and various other amenities of life. The government should try to obtain land from these companies and make it available to our returned men. These men should not have to go back thirty, forty or fifty miles from a railroad to settle on provincial land unless they wish to do so. In many cases these men would prefer to have land closer to railroad facilities, closer to markets and in places where they could receive better medical attention and have better school facilities for their children.
The fourth thing which I suggest the government should do is to permit a settler to use the SI,200 which he receives under the act for stock and equipment cooperatively with other settlers. Anyone who has had anything to do with farming knows how far SI,200 will go to-day in buying stock and equipment; it will just not go anywhere. The average farm in eastern Canada has at least $3,000 to $4,000 worth of stock and equipment. The average grain farm in western Canada has from $5,000 to $7,000 worth of equipment. If four or five returned men were allowed to pool their $1,200 cooperatively to buy equipment they could then purchase a reasonably economic unit with which to operate their holdings.
It was suggested in the committee that this could be done by each one buying his own equipment and then lending it to the others. Anyone who has been on a farm knows that that would not work out. There is mucn heavier upkeep on one piece of equipment than on another. A man may have a seed drill costing $400 and the upkeep would be quite small. Another man would have a binder upon which the upkeep would be higher. A third man might have an engine upon which the upkeep would be still higher. The only successful way to pool the use of equipment is cooperatively, to have the equipment owned and operated by the group.
Another way in which the settler could be assisted would be to make available tools, trucks or other equipment which are now under the control of War Assets Corporation. These should be made available to the settler direct without having to go through two or three hands with the consequent commissions having
to be paid. When the Minister of Munitions and Supply was before the committee he stated that the Department of Veterans Affairs would be given an opportunity to purchase this equipment. I suggest that the branch having to do with the Veterans' Land Act appoint a purchasing agent who could go to War Assets Corporation and obtain such equipment as may be used on the farm.
I know something of what it is to try to operate a farm with poor equipment. I tried to repair machinery which I had obtained under the old soldier settler board for the first four or five years I was on the land; I tried to work with a monkey-wrench and a piece of baling wire, but I found it discouraging. There are millions of dollars worth of tools and equipment now in the various camps and air force depots across Canada which could be used to good effect by the settlers who will be settled under this act. I strongly urge the minister to appoint a purchasing agent who could make out a list of what would be a reasonable set of tools for a settler. Then purchases could be made from War Assets Corporation and these tools made available to settlers who may want them.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
He could not carry on without baling wire.
Mr. WRIGHT; He will probably need a lot of baling wire as well. A farmer to-day has to be a jack of all trades. He has to be a motor mechanic; he has to be a blacksmith; he has
to be a carpenter; he has to be a tinsmith, and he has to be many other things. He would find things much more pleasant and helpful if he had the necessary equipment to do the job.
Many of these settlers are coming to the local offices set up under the Veterans' Land Act where they are shown what land is available. This land may not be in the district in which they want to settle. They are then told to go out, secure a suitable piece of land and report to the office. If the price is suitable, if the land is found to be reasonably good, the application will be considered. But it costs the returned man money to go out and look for land. I would suggest that some facilities be provided for settlers who are going out to look for land. At least a car should be placed at their disposal so that they can go out and select their land. Most of these boys have not too much money, and they will have to pay ten per cent of the cost and meet other expenses until they become established.
With respect to the small holdings, perhaps at the present time it cannot be avoided, but most of the building on these small holdings is being done by large contractors, who will

Veterans Land Act
put up twenty or thirty or forty or a hundred or two hundred houses, which are then sold to the returned men. Perhaps that is the only way in which this scheme can be operated at the present time. But just as soon as that method can be changed I would suggest to the minister that the veteran be given an opportunity and assisted to build his own home. With most of the successful cooperative housing schemes that we have in Canada, the measure of their success has largely been the measure in which the individual himself took part in the building of his own home. In cooperative housing schemes in the mining and fishing centres of Nova Scotia, for instance, groups of men would get together, study their own housing problems and then plan and build their own homes. In that way they built a home that was much cheaper and much more satisfactory to them as individuals than any house built by a large contractor could have been.
There are a large number of men returning this winter, and many of them will be out of a job. I would suggest that the department organize them where they want to go on small holdings and have study groups to study their housing problems and plans for their homes or small businesses which they wish to establish, and then get them to work on these things themselves. In that way you would find a much better satisfied group of people than if you put them into houses built for them by large contractors. There would be more personal satisfaction for the men themselves who had helped to build their homes with their own hands and more satisfaction for their wives who had helped to plan their own homes. There is nothing which gives more stability to a community or to a country than the ownership of a piece of land and the building of your own home. When you have planned and built your home yourself you do not leave it lightly. You will find a job in that community and remain there in all probability for the rest of your life. If such a plan were adopted I believe that it would stabilize, to some extent, at least, the fluctuations of population, the travelling from place to place by men looking for jobs.
These are just a few suggestion which we believe should be incorporated in the present act. We feel that when the house next meets we must be given an opportunity to review this act once more to study some of the suggestions that have been brought forward and to bring them to the attention of the government perhaps in the form of resolutions from the committee so that we can get action upon them.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I wish to express my
pleasure at having been on the veterans affairs committee. It has been an interesting experience to me. I have been interested to notice the non-partisan way in which the committee faced its problems and I hope it is a good omen for the future. I am sure of this: when we come to deal with the difficult problems that will face us, if we face them in the spirit of the committee, I have no fear for the future.
I wish personally to express my thanks to the minister, and to the officials of his department for their excellent cooperation in dealing with veterans and related questions in my own constituency. I am particularly interested in this amending bill that has been brought down, and for this reason particularly, that a large number of returned men in British Columbia will welcome the legislative powers given in section 6. That is the section which makes it possible to make capital grants to veterans settling on provincial lands. I believe that this section will prove to be one of the most successful of the whole act. I have on several occasions heard people minimize this form of settlement, but 1 think the future will prove that a greater percentage of men have been settled satisfactorily under this section than any other section of the Act.
In my own district we have large numbers of men who are interested in part-time farming in association with lumbering, mining, trapping and, in some cases, prospecting. I am not pleading the case of the capitalist farmer who requires a $10,000 starting investment, but the case of the proletarian farmer, as I am a socialist. We have large numbers of these in the interior of British Columbia who would like to have a small acreage of land and keep a cow, a pig or two and cultivate a few acres of fruit and hay and who, having some other occupation, will be able to make a satisfactory living. I am pleased to see this section incorporated in the act. I would ask the minister to do everything possible to see that an agreement is reached with the government of British Columbia, so that men wishing to settle under this section may be able to do so at the first opportunity. I have heard mentioned on one or two occasions that the settlement of these men would have to wait until the dominion-provincial conference had concluded. I do not see why that should be necessary, and I hope that the minister will do what he can to see that an agreement is reached with British Columbia, so that the men who are waiting to take advantage of this section can go on provincial land in the near future.
Veterans Land Act

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether the grants work out equally for the man who pays $6,000 for his farm and for the man who pays $5,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: It depends upon whether he puts it all into land or part into machinery. If he puts it all into land he does not get as much as if he also buys machinery. The entire cost of machinery up to $1,200 is ultimately cancelled if the veteran carries out his contract. If none is put into machinery he does not get cancellation in regard to the machinery. It all depends on the amount invested in machinery.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: He gets it all in land or land and machinery?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: He could put $1,000 of it into machinery and $5,000 into land, and then he would get a cancellation of the machinery in addition to cancellation on the land.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: It does not work out in the same way?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: No.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: How would that apply to soldiers who are taking advantage of provincial legislation and getting their farms free after living on them for ten years? Take, for example, the plan in Alberta, where they have agreed to set aside a certain amount of land, and after the soldier has lived there for ten years, with no taxes to pay on it or anything, he is given free title to that land; would the soldier there be entitled to this grant for buying machinery, cattle and equipment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Under the terms of the agreement he can get up to $2,320, and of course that can be used for the purposes set out in the act.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: That is the direct grant? That is what the hon. member called a while ago the free grant?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: That is the maximum he could get if he were using the assistance to buy machinery and land, and if he goes under the agreement with a province he can get the maximum amount of $2,320 for such purposes as clearing the land, purchase of buildings, purchase of live stock, machinery and so on, as set out in section 6 of the bill.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: While the hon. member to my left has been putting in a silent plug for the province of Alberta.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: They took the lead.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: -would it be possible for the parliamentary assistant to indicate the provinces which already have agreements with the Department of Veterans Affairs?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: As I remember it, Saskatchewan and Alberta.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: And British Columbia?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: British Columbia, as I remember, is not yet included in those with an agreement, but they are negotiating.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Just a few words in support of what the hon. member for Melfort has said about what he regards as the inadequacy of some provisions of the Veterans' Land Act. He has stated the views of this particular group, and it is not my purpose to supplement his remarks in that connection. But I would say this in so far as the activities of the committee on veterans' affairs are concerned: I feel that that committee has done an excellent job, not because I was one of them-

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Partly because-?

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Yes, partly. I do not think I have worked on any committee which has done such excellent work in such a short space of time. I believe I am right in saying that some thirty meetings or more were held, most of them of two hours' or more duration; they were conducted on a non-partisan basis, and the debates were more or less cutting across party lines every day. I would commend to the minister the suggestion that it would be an excellent thing if that committee, or one just as nearly like it as possible, could continue the work on behalf of the veteran, because I do not think there is any legislation before the house to-day or likely to come before the house in the near future which will be more important.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: We will appoint the same committee.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
One of the most commendable amendments of the Veterans Land Act is that which has to do with the extension of the provisions of the act to our Indian veterans of this war. Some of these Indian boys served in two wars, and they did an excellent job; they fought for our democratic principles; and I believe that this amendment which extends the provisions of the act to the Indian veteran is a step in the direction of granting full rights of citizenship to this fine body of people. By failing to provide for them we were guilty of a certain discrimination against a people who have always sacrificed for Canada when they were required to do so. They have been called to the colours at least three times in not a great many years, and they have acquitted themselves most commendably. I feel that by removing that

Veterans Land Act
act of discrimination against them, in so far at least as the Veterans' Band Act is concerned, we are doing something for which this country will acclaim the work of the veterans affairs committee and this house of parliament. Not only is it a fair and just thing to do, but it is a step to eliminate as much as we can this thorn in our flesh which we call racial discrimination. I hope that the work of committees of this kind will be extended and will bear fruit along the same lines in other sessions.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Most of those who have spoken on this bill this afternoon have been people on the opposition side of the house; but since in this committee the question of opposition does not arise, perhaps I should not have used that word. I think everyone who has spoken this afternoon has referred in complimentary terms to the cooperation of the committee and its lack of partisanship; indeed, most of them have spoken in complimentary terms of the cooperation received from the minister, the chairman, and the officials of the department. I know that both the minister and the chairman are much too modest to acknowledge even these compliments in the committee of the house. But as one of the supporters of the government, one who by the way, has sat on all or most of these committees since 1936, I would say that the debate this afternoon has been truly indicative of the interest of that committee in the veterans themselves and of the uniform desire of the members of that committee to really accomplish something.
However, it is not primarily of the things which we have jointly accomplished that I wish to speak at the moment. I should like to suggest to the minister and the committee what, it seems to me, remains to be done. One of the most important things which this committee will have to do when we meet again, as I understand we shall do, is to define, more accurately than we have been able to do in any except the first bill which they brought in this year, what amounts to a dishonourable discharge from the service, and to make sure that the application of that particular discharge does not diminish the benefits which are available. For instance, I am told that at the present time it is impossible, or most unlikely, for anyone who has been dishonourably discharged from the service to be established under the Veterans' Land Act, and yet I am pretty sure that there are worse disqualifications than dishonourable discharge. It might be that a man is dishonourably discharged for an act of insubordination, beating up the sergeant-major, or something of that description, which from a military point of
view might justify dishonourable dismissal from the service in order to make an example and to preserve discipline. The same pugnacious tendencies might not be any handicap to a man who is attempting to reestablish himself on a prairie farm. I think the word should go out to the interested veterans across the country that the committee are seriously concerned about that particular phase of rehabilitation and reestablishment, that it is not a dead issue, that we are united in the committee to see that when we meet again it will have further consideration, and that we shall more definitely define this provision in all the various enactments on the subject in this parliament.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: A few minutes ago the hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned a few things about the government of British Columbia and the dominion government coming to an agreement with regard to lands offered by the dominion government. Could the minister give us a statement regarding the matter, because I have taken exception to the conditions put in the offers of grants by the British Columbia government, and I have predicted that the plan will not be a success, owing to the regulations or the requirements for entry on the million acres which they are providing. One of the requirements is that any returned soldier taking advantage of the scheme must have enlisted from the province of British Columbia.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I objected to that.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I think a protest should be made against it. At the present time there are being discharged in Vancouver greater numbers of soldiers than originally enlisted from the Pacific coast. I feel sure that many of these men would like to take advantage of that offer; and I can say this without fear of successful contradiction, that those who have been raised in Vancouver and in the Fraser valley will not be very keen to go up into that district where the million acres which have been offered are located. They will not go there, and those who come to the province and would like to go there are debarred by these regulations of the provincial government. This can be said in fairness. The men who offered their lives did not offer them solely for British Columbia but for the whole of Canada, and yet they cannot take advantage of the regulations if they did not enlist from that province. I do not know whether the minister cares to explain it, but it is my information that that is one reason why the agreement has not been completed between the provincial government and the dominion. If so, steps should be taken and every argu-
Veterans Land Act

ment used to persuade the provincial government to amend the regulation, because I think it is deplorable.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: The minister should also consider doing the same thing under federal legislation that the province has been trying to do by provincial statute in the effort to assist returned men. The federal government could easily give land to the soldiers without compelling them to buy it. They could make a grant of the land. Surely if the provincial government can so arrange its affairs as to give land outright to a soldier after he has lived on it for ten years, without an accumulation of taxes, and without one cent of debt; if the province in its small way can do that, the federal government can certainly do the same throughout Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I am in entire agreement with the suggestion of the hon. member for New Westminster. I do not think there should be any regional limitation upon any land settlement of veterans in Canada. The whole question is one of suitability of the soil, economic availability of it, and suitability of the settler. We have gone through all this land very carefully, and it is going to cost the settler a great deal of money for the clearing of much of the land, so that I fear that in a great deal of this land there may be placed on the settler a burden such as was imposed upon him in 1919 and 1920, when too high prices were paid for land. If any agency or government were prepared to have it cleared, giving the benefit of the clearing to the settler, it would be a different question. I may tell my hon. friend that we have reviewed all that land. There are areas there that can be developed of course, but in many cases, I fear, unless one government or another assumes the cost of clearing the land itself it will be an impossible burden on the settler.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Surely the minister
knows that Alberta has suggested an arrangement between the federal government and the government of that province to do the very thing he asks. Why cannot the federal government come and assist the government of Alberta? It would not cost the returned man one cent, because the proposal is for the federal and provincial governments to take that responsibility. If Alberta can do it, I am sure the other provinces can do it, and I do not see why the federal government cannot render such assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: We have gone very far with Alberta, as the agreement which has been signed will indicate.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: But they are a progressive province and you should follow their lead.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I had not intended to say anything about the situation in British Columbia until section 6 of the bill came up for discussion, but seeing that other members have already brought up the matter and that the minister has dealt with it I should like to say a few words. I am convinced that both the dominion government and the government of British Columbia are trying to do their utmost to help the veteran to get on the land. Some suggestion has been made in the remarks we have heard that the provincial government is not doing the fair thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I did not suggest that at all.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Certainly there is something wrong somewhere, and perhaps both governments are to be condemned for not getting together and entering into an agreement. The provincial government over two years ago set aside a million acres, which, as I understand, was to be given free to the veterans. The provincial government, rightly or wrongly, restricted that to veterans who had enlisted in British Columbia. I think they should have asked for some provision such as priority to the men who enlisted in British Columbia. One reason they took that position was that so many men kept moving into the province who had not enlisted from British Columbia, although we have the highest enlistment record in Canada. I believe that Prince Edward Island and British Columbia are equal. I do not doubt that some change could now be made, that the provincial government would be willing to alter their provisions, but the British Columbia legislature is meeting in another two months and time is of the greatest importance. This disagreement must not be allowed to go on; the two governments must get together without further delay. The provincial government is hoping to have these lands opened up. I believe the idea is to open up frontier lands. The dominion government do not want to put veterans on frontier lands, and there is a difference of opinion there. Why would it not be possible to make some arrangement whereby the provincial government would help with the clearing of the land? That would obviate one of the difficulties.
In the committee I formed the opinion that perhaps the director and his staff had given up too soon. This scheme has now become largely, or at any rate partly, a housing scheme, whereas it was intended originally to be a scheme

Veterans Land Act
for settling veterans on farms. But the figures given by the director show that there are far more veterans being settled on small holdings in the suburbs of the large cities than are being settled on the farms, and it may be that the attention of the director and his staff is concentrated too much on these small holdings, beneficial as they are. Mind you, they mean a lot of work. They bring up all sorts of problems, and I imagine they are causing the director far more concern than settlement on farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Quite true.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The situation in British
Columbia may be caused by the fact that the director is paying too much attention to the small holdings on the outskirts of cities and not enough to the settling of veterans on farms. According to the figures he has given, and they are illuminating-they will be found at page 624 of the proceedings of the veterans affairs committee-he estimates that up to the end of 1946, that is after the war will have been over for a year and half, there will be settled under the Veterans' Land Act across the whole of Canada only 6,420 farmers, as against 10,225 small holders settling in the suburbs of cities and 825 as commercial fishermen, or a total of 17,470. That is less than half the number of men who, it is estimated, will have applied for help under this act. He gave the figures for the applicants. It is indicated that the numbers who have applied already are 14,276 for farming establishments, and just over 6,400 will be settled up to the end of 1946 ; 20,040 have applied for small holdings, and about half that number will have been settled by the end of next year. Veterans to the number of 1,464 have applied for help as commercial fishermen, and only 825 will have been settled by the end of next year, so that the whole scheme is in danger of bogging down and of becoming a housing scheme.
The minister himself suggested in the committee the other day that he thought there should be one housing authority in Canada to look after all the problem of housing and not have it divided up between his Department of Veterans Affairs working under the Veterans' Land Act in connection with those small holdings, the Department of Reconstruction, working under Wartime Housing, and the Department of Finance working under the National Housing Act. I think he was quite right; but in any event the government must not overlook the fact that this is primarily an act to settle veterans on the farms. So far as the situation in British Columbia is concerned that objective has not been met at the
present time, and it will not be met until the two governments reach some sort of agreement. I am hopeful that the airing of this difficulty first in the committee, and then in the house-I am sure it will be aired in the press-will assist the governments to get together. Only in that way can they bring to the veterans the benefits that have been earned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
There are one or two things I wish to mention. In regard to the governments which have made agreements, I forgot to mention that the government of Manitoba has also made an agreement. In regard to British Columbia, I would point out that our department is pressing for an agreement but is handicapped by the fact that this provision which has been mentioned by the hon. member for New Westminster is part of the statute law of British Columbia and they cannot do anything until they have that law changed. That has been the difficulty, but our department is pressing for an agreement as hard as it can.
While I am on my feet I should like to express deep and sincere appreciation to those who have made constructive speeches this afternoon; also to those who, while having strong opinions about various matters, have refrained from speaking so that we might hope to get these two bills through this afternoon. It has been a great privilege to me to sit on the veterans affairs committee, and I wish to thank 'those who cooperated on the committee and also those who cooperated in the house in order that these two bills might go through as they have this afternoon.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I was one of those who refrained from speaking, and perhaps I may have an opportunity to ask one or two elementary questions now. The parliamentary assistant to the minister referred to an agreement with Manitoba. Could he outline that agreement in a minute or two? Then I have another question with respect to the numbers who have settled on the farm.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
