speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on Saturday evening when my departmental estimates were called a few moments before closing time the hon. member for Humboldt asked me if I would make a statement on the reorganization work in connection with the Department of Trade and Commerce for the last year or two. He asked that I refer specially to the trade representatives that we have in the various countries, where they are located and the general developments within the Department of Trade and Commerce looking to Canada's trade position in the postwar period. In submitting the estimates for my department I am therefore making a brief statement on some of the more important aspects of the work which was carried out by the department last year and on its plans to help maintain Canada's place as one of the world's great trading nations.
To meet the new problems which face us in world trade, the division in the department formerly known as the commercial intelligence service has been reorganized and is now known as the foreign trade service. It is under the direction of the new deputy minister of the department, Mr. M. W. Mackenzie. It has six main branches, the trade commissioners service, the export division, the import division, the commercial relations and foreign tariffs division, the trade publicity division, and the wheat and; grain division. I should like to comment briefly on the duties of each of these divisions.
We intend to have trade commissioners stationed in every major trading centre in the world where the appointment of such a representative will contribute to the enlargement
of Canadian commerce. The offices in Paris and Brussels were reopened some months ago and trade commissioners have been assigned to the Netherlands and to Norway. An office will also be opened in the near future in Stockholm, and a trade commissioner is being sent to Greece to be attached to the embassy there and to supervise our trade relations in Turkey and the Balkan countries as well. Following the resumption of private trade with French North and West Africa, a trade commissioner has been sent to Algiers on a special mission to explore trading opportunities there and to establish sound trade connections for Canadian exporters interested in that market. An office will be opened in Venezuela early in 1946.
A senior trade commissioner has been assigned to Australia and an additional officer appointed in New Zealand. A special representative is to proceed to the Netherlands East Indies to assist in reopening our trade with that area. We are sending a senior officer to South Africa early next year to strengthen our representation there. Specialist trade commissioners in agricultural and forestry products have also been appointed, and they will have duties not only in the United Kingdom but in Europe and elsewhere.
Then, we have been fortunate in securing the services of some excellent young men from the armed forces as assistant trade commissioners. In conformity with government policy, applications were considered only from men with overseas service. We have been highly gratified with the number and calibre of these young men who wish to continue to serve Canada abroad. Six assistant trade commissioners and one specialist trade commissioner have already proceeded to foreign posts; two more are leaving shortly; fourteen additional assistant trade commissioners are now in training. Nine additional assistants will join the department in March or April. This makes a total of thirty new assistant trade commissioners who are now at work or will join the trade commissioner service shortly. This indicates the importance we attach to having a strong body of commercial representatives abroad.
Before the war we had thirty-four offices abroad, manned by thirty-five trade commissioners and twenty-five assistant trade commissioners. During the war the number of offices declined1, of course, by the enforced closing of those in Berlin, Oslo, Rotterdam, Brussels, Paris, Milan, Singapore, Hong Kong. Shanghai and Tokyo. To-day we have thirty-one offices located abroad, with forty trade commissioners and seven assistant trade com-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
missioners assigned to them. As I have just said, we intend to establish offices almost immediately in Sweden, Greece, Venezuela and the Netherlands East Indies; we shall have representation in Italy as soon as practicable, and our offices in Singapore, Hong Kong and Shanghai will be reopened as soon as the trading position permits.
We have had only two specialist trade commissioners in London for some time past. This phase of our work abroad will be expanded; in addition to those officers who have devoted their attention to animal products and fruit, we will send a timber trade commissioner to the United Kingdom, and it is our intention to appoint a fisheries products trade commissioner at a later date. We are also selecting officers with agricultural training to be assigned to other countries, including north Europe, Argentina and Australia.
Our trade commissioners will be responsible not only for the sale of Canadian goods in the territories in which they are stationed, but also for the encouragement of imports into Canada in recognition of the principle that trade can flourish only if it is mutually profitable and is being conducted1 on a twoway basis. The promotion of exports abroad will, of course, remain the primary responsibility of our trade commissioners, but their new and enlarged duties give them greater opportunities for rendering service to Canada and in helping to establish a sound balance between our export and' our import policies.
We have recently held a special conference of our trade commissioners of Latin-America. Despite the restrictions on normal trade imposed by war conditions, Canada's trade with Latin-America has shown a seventy per cent increase in exports and a 400 per cent increase in imports. It should be emphasized that this remarkable increase in imports has taken place because the Latin-American countries have provided many essential raw materials for Canada's manufacturing industries during the war. Our exports for the first nine months of this year are nearly double our total exports for all of 1939. Our export trade with the countries in Latin-America I visited in 1941 as head of a special Canadian trade mission, that is Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Uruguay, has more than doubled. For the first nine months ending September 1945, our export trade with these countries amounted to nearly $24,000,000 as compared with $10,000,000 for a similar period in 1939. We hope soon to reestablish direct shipping routes to the Latin-American countries instead of routing our goods through the United States, and this should increase our trade with Latin-American countries to a substantial degree.

The figures as shown in the return in connection with our imports from Latin-American countries are misleading inasmuch as no record is shown of the very large quantities of imports that come to us through United States channels. From one country alone, Colombia, a most important volume of merchandise is imported to Canada which does not show in our ordinary Canadian figures.
Our trade with Latin America was perhaps not given as much attention in the past as this great market merited. We believe that Canada is destined to enjoy a steadily growing trade with these nations. It may not be too optimistic to believe that our export trade with Latin America can reach $200 million a year in the immediate future, provided that Canadian exporters pay the attention to this market which its potential importance warrants. Our export trade with Mexico alone, for example, we hope will rise to $60 million a year.
The export planning division was organized in August, 1943, under the direction of one of the department's senior trade commissioners recalled from overseas duty for this purpose. The principal function of the export planning division has been to prepare a programme, in cooperation, where necessary, with the combined planning authorities in Washington, of exports from Canada of essential commodities required by overseas countries to maintain their national economies. The division also arranged that even where goods were in short supply there at least was a movement of merchandise to our old markets, so that Canada could maintain at least token trade with our old customers during the prevailing period of scarcity. The results of this policy are already evident in the pattern of our postwar trade. This division in 1945 prepared some seventy commodity and country programmes. This work involved close cooperation with the appropriate combined board in Washington and with the external trade advisory committee in Ottawa on which various departments are represented.
With the organization of a foreign trade service in the department effective November 1, 1945, the export planning division ceased to exist. The work of the division will largely be absorbed in the new export division which will have special responsibilities in the planning of our trade with the British empire, the West Indies, Europe, France, the far east and Latin America.
Since the import division was established last year, more than 1,700 Canadian agents and import houses have registered with it. The division received1 numerous inquiries from

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Canadian importers for information on foreign supply conditions, foreign export controls, shipping regulations, foreign price levels and currency exchange restrictions. The import division has been working in close cooperation with the various foreign government trade representatives in Canada, and much business as a result has come to this country which might otherwise have been lost.
The division of commercial relations and that of foreign tariffs have, recently been combined to perform the work that was formerly done by each division separately or in various other parts of the department. The primary duty of the foreign tariffs section is to promote Canadian export trade by furnishing information on customs tariffs and other trade regulations as they prevail in the world with particular reference to Canadian trade. In the negotiation of trade treaties the commercial relations division bears special responsibili-;ies. It has been most active in studying our trade with the United Kingdom, the United States, the sterling area and Latin-America. The results of this long preparatory work will be evident in the very near future.
We are planning a notable expansion in our trade publicity programme including the work of the exhibitions branch, which has necessarily been curtailed during the war years.
While Canada's Mutual Aid programme commenced in September, 1943, the 1944-45 fiscal year was the first full fiscal year of operation for the wheat and grain division.
, Mutual Aid operations for the division began with the shipment of wheat and flour to the United Kingdom. The imported cereals division of the United Kingdom ministry of food continued their purchases as agents of the department, while this division undertook responsibility for the disbursement of Mutual Aid and United Kingdom cash funds in settlement of deliveries against ministry of food contracts.
In August, 1943, flour was first shipped to the U.S.S.R. under a Soviet credit agreement. Upon the exhaustion of these funds in January, 1944, shipments were made under Mutual Aid, and toward the end of that year wheat cargoes were added to the Russian programme.
Beginning in November, 1944, as part of Canada's military relief contribution, a substantial volume of wheat moved overseas. Here again the division assumed responsibility for disbursement of military occupation relief funds.
The shipment of gift wheat to Greece for relief commenced in August, 1942, at a rate of approximately 15,000 long tons a month. Grain accounts were approved for payment by the 47696-209
division from funds set up under the War Appropriation Act. Relief wheat shipments continued up until April 1,1945, when UNRRA assumed full financial responsibility for the distribution of relief supplies in Greece. I had the privilege of mentioning once before the reception which Canada's gift of wheat to Greece received in that country at the time of her great necessity. People in high government circles in Greece informed us that the shipment of Canadian wheat to Greece actually saved hundreds of thousands of lives.
Relief wheat loadings were resumed as part of Canada's contribution to UNRRA. In addition to wheat, substantial quantities of Canadian flour were also included in the UNRRA programme. Flour contracts were placed directly with the mills against UNRRA purchase orders, with the division also handling disbursement of funds for UNRRA account.
The Exports Credits Insurance Act which was passed on August 15, 1944-in my reference to this act I shall deal only with that part which comes directly under the Department of Trade and Commerce, namely, part I-provided for the setting up of a corporation to insure exporters against the main risks of loss involved in foreign trade. This corporation, called the Exports Credits Insurance Corporation, was proclaimed on November 21, 1944. Two of the senior officers of the corporation visited the United Kingdom this summer to study the operations and experience of the export credits guarantee department which functions there under the board of trade-a government department-and which has operated successfully for the past twenty-six years. The results of this long British experience are being incorporated in the policy and practice of the Exports Credits Insurance Corporation. Canadian exporters from all parts of Canada have taken out policies with the corporation and these include small business houses as well as large concerns. Individual annual sales volumes covered by the insurance range from $50,000 to $3,000,000. Commodities covered by the policies already written include raw materials, agricultural products and manufactured goods.
During the last fiscal year the dominion bureau of statistics, in addition to carrying out its normal duties, had to discharge heavy responsibilities in preparing statistical information required by the various branches of government service engaged in our war effort. In addition it carried out detailed studies to meet the needs of post-war reconstruction.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

An important item of the bureau's programme is the development of improved service to Canadian business. It is planned to issue monthly statistical tables showing the production, shipments and stocks of the more important commodities. This new practice will result in the early publication of current statistics required by Canadian business. At the same time this up-to-date statistical service will enable various departments of the government to have special data to assist them in the formulation of policy.
It will be recalled that the government white paper of April, 1945, on employment and income set up as a practical and desirable target for our post-war exports the figure of one and three-quarter billion dollars annually at current prices for merchandise exports and non-monetary gold. This would be about sixty per cent above the pre-war level in dollar value but only about fifteen per cent higher in the amount of goods exported. We believe, on the strength of our present trading relationships and future trends in our trade which we can now define, that this objective will be realized. The promotion of our trade is in the very forefront of the government's entire programme of reconstruction, and the Department of Trade and Commerce is discharging direct responsibilities in helping to realize the objectives of this programme.
Mr. Chairman, I have covered some of the reorganization work which has been taking place in the Department of Trade and Commerce in the last year or two, so that it will be in a position to promote Canada's trade, which we feel is wholly necessary to the maintenance of our national prosperity.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is indeed a pleasure to have an opportunity of thanking the minister for the comprehensive statement he has made in connection with the affairs of his department. I was thinking, during the time that he was giving us that interesting resume, that it is too bad he stopped me as soon as he did on Saturday evening after I had put a few questions on the record as to what we would be interested in, because if he had waited a little while longer he would have had so much subject material that he would have made a record speech this evening, if he had done with the rest of it as he did with the questions I put to him.
While I am in the mood for passing compliments I will continue in the same strain for a little while. Some weeks ago I had the pleasure of complimenting the Minister of Agriculture in connection with a little booklet which his department was putting out and which is of great service and information to those of us who are interested in the pro-

duction of live stock. To-night, first, because I do not want to be accused of playing favourites, and, second, because I really do appreciate what the department has done in this direction, I wish to mention the booklet, which is called the "Monthly Review of the Wheat Situation," put out by the department under the authority of the minister. I thank the minister and the officials of his department for the work which is connected with it and for the comprehensive information which it contains. But in that connection I would say that there is one criticism I have to offer. As the government through the agency of the Canadian wheat board has handled the product of the labour, one might say the sweat, of the people who produced that wheat, there should be included in this book or a similar book, at least once a year, a full accounting of the activities of the wheat board. I make that suggestion to the minister, because it is of great importance to the people who produce Canada's wheat. The book is of real value to those of us farmers who have an opportunity to peruse it from time to time.
The department is also issuing other booklets and information. The minister referred to certain statistics concerning other dealings, especially those relating to Canadian business. I would suggest that the minister and his department prepare in summarized form for the information of members as well as the public generally, a sort of over-all summary of the business of the country. While I appreciate his view that some of us are especially interested in wheat, we want him to understand that we are also much interested in the business of Canada as a whole, and would value an opportunity of seeing such an over-all picture from time to time.
I listened with great attention and a considerable amount of pleasure to the minister's statement in connection with our trade representatives in different parts of the world. It is an evidence that the government recognizes its responsibility and the necessity of preparing and being prepared for the years in the immediate future. Especially was I pleased to observe the note which crept into the minister's report where he stated that the duties of these men would also now include matters respecting importations into Canada as well as the exportations. I was pleased with that, because we have known for a long time that if we are to have a healthy condition of trade it must be a trade which will balance. If it does not balance, eventually we shall find ourselves confronted with a condition in which it has become so unbalanced as to be unwieldy and unmanageable.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
But I would suggest that, as much as we as a nation are concerned with the exporting of our surplus goods and with importations for our requirements, we must not forget that part of the trade which is of vital concern to every Canadian, namely, the trade within the boundaries of our own country. We have in this dominion a tremendous consuming -power. I am sure I am speaking not only for myself but for every member of this house when I say that never again do we want a condition to develop in this country whereby apples in British Columbia are rotting and children in the prairie provinces cannot get apples; where people in the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec have their factories closed because they cannot dispose of the goods which they produce, while in other parts of the country there are people whose supply of those goods is most meagre, the least that they can get along with. We do not want to have a return of that condition in Canada, and consequently trade within our own country is of the greatest importance. I suggest that the proper approach to that question is, first of all, the recognition of the importance of a little planning. I do not want hon. members to be frightened when we use that term. We must use a little ordinary common sense and business judgment. In arriving at what the requirements of the people are, we must be able to plan how to supply those requirements. I suggest, therefore, that planning is not something to run away from, but something that is simply good, plain, ordinary business judgment.
We need to find out, in the first place, how much the people need of the various products we can produce, how much they need of the various things we can manufacture, and then proceed as far as possible to supply our own home market and to see to it that the people within the boundaries of this country have an opportunity to consume to the fullest extent. Then, when that is accomplished, it devolves upon the Department of Trade and Commerce to provide us with markets to which we can export our surpluses and, in return for those surpluses, we must be prepared' to channel back into the country, by means of exchange in one way or another, the things that we cannot economically produce in Canada and which we need here in order to round out a full and high standard of living.
I contend that within the boundaries of a country like Canada the standard of living that the people will have depends entirely upon the productive ability of the nation. It is true that we cannot consume all our wheat, but we can certainly use other things for 47696-209i
which wheat can be exchanged. We can use things that are not easily produced in this country, and that is where trade will help our people to make the fullest possible use of the things they produce.
As we go on we find ourselves sometimes in a peculiar position, and I would suggest that in planning production and distribution of the goods we require within the country we must again use a little more common sense than was used in the thirties when there existed the condition to which I referred a moment ago. Even now we are in the midst of another difficult situation. Hon. members will recall, for instance, a statement which was made in the house that in the neighbourhood of eighty per cent of the lumber of the country was being exported.

speechtext: Forty-two per cent.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am corrected by one of my colleagues who says it was forty-two per cent. I thought it was higher; but, even so, forty-two per cent is a considerable amount. We were given an explanation of that, but we find ourselves in this position to-day. There are in Canada thousands of people who are urgently in need of suitable living quarters, and yet at the same time a vast amount of our timber is being exported. In one of the explanations given to us we were told that we cannot very well cut down on the export of that timber because we need the dollar to balance our trade or to carry on our trade. Here is the ironical situation. At the same time we are importing coal from the same country to which we are exporting lumber. We are importing coal to help our people to keep warm in houses which they do not have-a queer contradiction. There is a strange situation for you. It certainly -would help to balance our trade a little better if we used some more Alberta coal on the one side and a little more Nova Scotia coal on the other. It would help to keep our people in useful production and keep down the number of United States dollars that we need. If -we did that, then possibly we might have a few more sticks of lumber which we need in order to put up a few more houses to accommodate our people.
We must remember that the first call on the productive ability of our people is a decent standard of living. I do not want hon. members to misunderstand me when I make that statement. I was exceedingly pleased when the minister mentioned the quantity of foodstuffs that had been shipped through Mutual Aid to other countries and he referred to Greece. The thought came to me that this is truly a modern exemplification of casting one's bread upon the waters.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

I submit that the people of Canada are all not only prepared but anxious to give all the assistance they can to those who are in such dire need. In passing, I would remind the minister and hon. members that while our farmers are proud of the fact that they can play some little part in helping to make the provision of that food possible for people who need it so urgently, we farmers should not be asked to carry the entire load of these gifts.
The minister referred to the continuous expansion now taking place and mentioned the trade representatives to other countries. Again, I am pleased that he has taken such early action. It occurred to me that while going along in this way, there is still something lacking, and I hope the minister will not hold it against me too much for having that feeling. But there was something that I could not make click, and finally it struck me that possibly some branch of the department was lagging behind.
Let me put it in this way. I remember years ago when I was a small boy-possibly I should have been going to school at the time if there had been a school nearby-[DOT] when I was helping to break open my father's homestead which is part of the farm I am now on. I was driving a yoke of oxen hitched to the plough. We went down one side and laid over a furrow and came back the other side and laid another furrow. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I am sometimes reminded of my early experience when we want to get a little work done in this house. It is a slow process; but we kept plodding along and we got the furrows laid together.
Later on, in the middle twenties, I believe I was the first farmer east of Saskatoon who had a one-way plough that cut a strip eight and a half feet wide and would travel along at three and a half to four miles an hour. Later on, I again was the first farmer in my community to have a rubber-tired tractor and a rubber-tired combine. People used to come for miles around to see that rubber-tired tractor work, and they would say: "Well, Joe, it is working all right now, but wait until we get a little shower of rain and you will be hollering for someone with a lug tractor to come and pull you out." There are very few tractors going out into that part of the country to-day or were in the years gone by which are not equipped with rubber tires. The point I wish to drive home to the minister is that at this time when he is preparing to send trade envoys to different parts of the world he could send them in planes, if necessary, travelling at 500 miles an hour. We have those modern means of

transportation and communication, and yet there is too much of that old oxen-day psychology left in our trading.
I should like the minister to give consideration to bringing his department up to date. I ask him to bring it up to date where it will meet the requirements and our ability to make use of the modern means which are now at our disposal. I should like to see our trade representatives in different parts of the world advertising our goods. They should be looked upon as salesmen; they should also encourage trade coming the other way. I wish to bring to his attention and to the attention of the members of the committee that we have reached a different position- in the commerce of the world. We have now come to a time where we find nation after nation abandoning the idea of the different people interested in trade running here and there trying to sell their wares. They now sell as a nation. In other words, they sell to you and they buy from you in bulk quantities through a government board. I have no hesitation in asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the members of this committee to consider seriously if the time has not come-in fact in the opinion of some of us it is long overdue-when -we should have import and export boards which will in an intelligent and businesslike manner help the people who produce the wealth of the nation to export their surpluses and1 in return import the things they need over -and above the things they can produce.

When I heard the minister speak about more trade commissioners I said to myself, that is a good thing, that is a real step in the right direction. of handling this work, through their many brilliant salesmen, many of whom I have met. We, too, shall have to select the best we can.

In Ontario, of which I wish to speak for a few minutes, we have many great manufacturing cities. They will need every ounce of assistance-and perhaps that is not the right word, but if we take it collectively, and then add it all up, one will get the right idea-that the department can give.

speechtext:
Yes; and then there is
Buenos Aires, with a population of several millions. I look at pictures of these fine cities with their magnificant buildings and institutions, universities and halls, and I at once think of their requirements in the matter of vacuum cleaners, elevators, and all those things which enter into the construction of big buildings. There are multitudes of articles of that kind in the manufacture of which Canadians are expert. I have been wondering, myself, in what way our trade commissioners have been able to promote these various lines of sales. [Mr. MacNicol.l
Our American cousins can do it-and do do it. I hope we have been making some of those sales, and have followed the same methods.
We have Canadian manufacturers for a thousand and one lines of these goods which we could sell in other countries, including the people in South America, and I am wondering how we proceed to make those sales. Do we operate through trade commissioners? If so, are they qualified to lay out blue-prints as to how this or that equipment is to be installed. In my day that was the type of man I engaged. All the company engineers who went throughout Europe and America took their direction from me. They were qualified experts in their line, and they were able to get big orders. And of course big orders mean employment. That is what I am thinking about. I am thinking of the thousands of men back in Davenport riding, a great manufacturing riding, who make their living through the manufacture of goods. I am thinking of providing orders for factories in that and in all other manufacturing ridings, so that the men engaged in them can have jobs. That is going to be our great problem from now on. I have been thinking of that, and I hope the department will consider this matter.
Looking through the records only a few minutes ago, I found that in 1944 we made about a billion and a half dollars worth of machinery alone machinery made from iron and steel. That was tremendous production, but I am sure that to-day, with our enormously expanded production equipment in our great plants, we can surpass even that amount.
I have in mind one great plant in the constituency of Wentworth. That is one of the finest institutions in the world. I refer to the John Bertram Machinery company. That may not be the modern name for it, but that was what it was called when I used to be in business. Perhaps to-day it is called the Bertram Machinery company. They have a staff of about 4,000 and they are by far the largest permanent old-line machine tool industry in Canada.
That is only one of a dozen I could name. Only a few days ago I had occasion to go to a plant. I go to as many plants as I can, because I like visiting them. When I smell the oil and smell the steel curling from the lathes, I feel that I am -back home again, where I used to be years ago. That plant had an order for 200 big machines for shipment to Europe.
That is -only one company. Do our trade commissioners interest themselves in matters of that kind? I apn sure they do. Are they trying to get some of that new business with

Supply-Trade and Commerce
France? Are they getting business with Gar-many-because it has to be rebuilt? I am not one of those who wish to see Germany forever crushed. I cannot bring myself to a decision of that kind. They were our enemies,' but we defeated them, and we are told to forgive our enemies.
Germany, Belgium, France and all those other countries in Europe that have been destroyed will have to be rebuilt. There is big business over there. Their plants are destroyed. One of the nations-and I am not mentioning which one-has dismantled many of their plants and taken them to its own country. But plants will have to be reestablished, and we can get some of that business.
In what way are our trade commissioners in Canada qualified to describe these things to purchasers in Germany, France, Russia, Belgium, Holland, Italy or wherever they may go; will they have the qualifications to be able to explain just how these machines operate, what it will mean to them if they buy them, how much faster they go, how much more they can produce and how much they will cut down their cost of production? Mr. Chairman, you know that it was the ability to operate at a low cost of production that has enabled the many fine manufacturing plants in your city to expand. The same applies to my riding where there are many manufacturing institutions.
We hear a lot about foreign affairs and the foreign affairs committee; everybody wants to be on the foreign affairs committee. In my judgment the time has come to have a home affairs committee, and the bigger it is the better. After all, Canada is in the manufacturing business and it must sell at home seventy-five to eighty per cent of the goods produced in Canada. Canada is our greatest market. We want all the foreign business we can get, but our big market is the home market. When I was studying commerce at the university in the United States we were taught that the United States had to export only ten per cent of what it produced. That meant that it consumed the other ninety per cent at home. I got it into my mind at that time that home affairs were of vast importance, of much more importance than foreign affairs.
Of course I know that if we cannot sell our surplus products it cuts down the price and increases unemployment here at home. I am strong for foreign exports, but I am also strong for home exports to the various provinces in Canada. I should like the minister to tell us what his department is doing to promote sales in Canada. We must remember that every manufacturing country is going to
send its salesmen here-I have met them in the last two days-to place on the markets of Canada that which is being produced elsewhere. How are we to compete with them? Is this to be done through the Canadian manufacturers' association, that wonderful body of men which, despite everything that is said about them, has done so much to build up this country. I love those men who have done such great things for Canada and who have provided employment for so many hundreds of thousands of men. I am not going to enter into any argument on that phase, but I know that if you treat your men as they should be treated, and as I always treated them, they will produce more for you. If the workmen like the people they are working for they will do more work for them. After all, malingering and staying off the job does not cut down costs, and that is the main thing. You do not cut costs by cutting down your rate of wages in employment. You must keep men on the job working with earnest hearts so that the company they work for can make the best goods in the shortest time. When the minister speaks again I should like him to tell us what the department intends to do to promote sales in Canada. We must not forget that we shall be up against the ablest men that can be sent from other manufacturing countries, including the United States. They will be out to get a market in Canada. We cannot blame them, but we want to keep our own home market if we can, because that is the best for us. '

Colombia, Peru and Chile, and then there is the fine paved highway from Chile across to Buenos Aires.

Mr. Chairman, after
strolling around through Bretton Woods and looking back at Dumbarton Oaks, if I were not an experienced lumberman I might have got lost in the bush. I hope that what I shall say will be brief, constructive and cooperative.
I notice by this blue book that the costs of nearly every department are up, and in several instances trade is down. When you hire a man to do a job for you, you expect him to do a little better job if you give him a little more money, so that with these increased expenditures we shall expect some good work and more efficiency in the days to come.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I should like to speak of lumber particularly. I do not want to discuss agriculture, because the hon. member for Humboldt has spoken of the agricultural industry and I do not want to repeat what he said. When he ploughed that wide furrow and that narrow furrow he reminded me of my own political ancestors ploughing the straight and narrow furrow back in 1934. But I do' not want to go back to the bad years of the 1930's.
In the provinces of Ontario and Quebec the subsidies were taken off cordwood last fall, at a time when I think they should have been kept on, because at that period of the year we need to take out large quantities of cord-wood which would help our trade balance with the United States and be an off-set to our coal imports and such like.
It has been said that the returned men are not- going back to the bush. I want to contradict that, because I have ten boys back from overseas who are working in my bush operations at the present time.
The lumbermen are going ahead and taking out a certain amount of lumber. They produced lumber all through the war period and we can produce lumber in the peace period; in fact I am sure that a lot more can be produced in the future than in the past if the prices are right. You remember, sir, what happened in 1929 after the last war to practically all the lumber business in Canada. We have ceiling prices on lumber, and if you want the lumbermen to go ahead, floor prices should be set because the lumbermen are fearful of what happened before. But if you set floor prices and readjust your ceiling prices I am sure we can produce more lumber than before.
So far as soft woods are concerned, which are used in the building trades, there is very little of that for export. I would speak especially of hemlock. It costs more to produce hemlock than spruce or pine, and at the same time the price is lower. Hemlock, practically ninety-five per cent of which is used in the building trades for home consumption, should have better prices set, a price that would at least allow a man to take it out at cost. In the past few years we lumbermen have taken out hemlock more or less from patriotic motives. But the war is over and the same feeling does not exist. If you want lumber taken out for the building trades in Canada, raise the price of hemlock by two or three dollars a thousand and put in floor prices.
So far as building up our export trade is concerned, the higher grades of No. 1 common and better are the grades of hardwood we export. I would say that you should 47696-210
throw the quota system into the waste-paper basket and let us export our higher grades of hardwood. The lower grades of hardwood go to our flooring plants in Canada. Our largest business has been and will be with Great Britain. That trade with Great Britain was built up after the empire economic conference which was held here in Ottawa, and I think it would be a good thing if this government called such another empire conference. That was the turning point in the depression before. We are not saying that we have a depression now or that we are going to have one, but if it was good in the time of the depression it would be that much better now.
In his statement the minister did not clarify the matter of trading or exports with Great Britain and other nations and areas of the sterling bloc. Articles have been written on it, to the effect that a certain amount of our exports are being blocked by failure to obtain import permits into these countries. I should like the minister to clarify that before this debate ends.
As regards Canada's domestic exports, in October of this year they were valued at S228 million, as against approximately S314 million in October, 1944, a decrease of a little over twenty-seven per cent. Exports to the United States in October were $88| million in round figures; in October of last year they were S123 million, which is a decrease of approximately 24J per cent. On September 19 the minister tabled order in council P.C. 6122 setting the export price of wheat at $1.55, and he referred at that time to the obligation of Canada not to take advantage of the allies in time of need; he referred also to the matter of building good will in Europe. Along with that is coupled the guaranteed floor price of $1 a bushel on authorized deliveries of wheat in Canada up to 1945, with $1.25 remaining for the present year; that is, until July, 1946. The question I wish to ask the minister is this. Since the producer in Canada is the one who is compelled to take the lower price on account of the pegging, to create good will for all Canada, is that policy being followed in any other department with respect to any other commodity that is being sold abroad? For instance, with bacon, do you peg the price to Canada Packers regardless of the price of bacon in the export market and compel the packer to take a lower price, or do you allow the packer to get the top price, sell it abroad at the lower price, and then pay a subsidy? And what about lumber and other products in Canada?
47696-210J
As a result of this action, a good many wheat growers feel that the primary producer takes the rap, whereas, where you have manufactured products, such as lumber, the people who have monopolies are guaranteed the top price; the people of Canada pay it, and the taxpayers make up the difference. Why not treat one the same as the other?
Another point arises out of a report that appeared in the evening Citizen, and the minister will either deny it or let us know what the situation is. maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I wish to direct two or three questions to the minister, and particularly the matter that arose recently in Washington where the statement was made that by reason of loan arrangements between Great Britain and the United States the British preference on many commodities would be done away with in whole or in part. That is a matter which affects the welfare of this country to a large extent, and we on this side of the house, His Majesty's opposition, have always believed that one of the most important considerations for assuring the trade of this country was the maintenance of the British preferences.
I feel that on this subject the minister should give a complete statement to the house. I was very much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario. He pointed out that Britain had bought before the war two or three times the quantity of stuff that was shipped to Canada, and that the importance of trade with Britain cannot be exaggerated. We believe, therefore, that we have the right to know whether or not- and I appropriate the words without reference to the speaker-there has been any brazen interference with the British preference, whether such is contemplated, and what is being done by the minister in order to prevent
Supply-Trade and Commerce

a breach in the British preference, the maintenance of which is so necessary to our future prosperity.
Much is made of the necessity of maintaining our agricultural markets in Britain and on the continent, and all of us feel that is important. We also believe that everything should be done in the way of export of agricultural products to relieve Britain's monotonous ration that has prevailed during the war.
What is being done by this country to maintain these markets abroad, in agricultural products other than wheat? I realize that in part this does not come under the minister, but it is impossible to discuss any of these subjects without occasionally encroaching upon some other department. Are Canadians today permitted to ship from Canada parcels of agricultural products such as butter and cheese, tongue and bacon and the like? The reason I ask that is that within the last three or four weeks, while the Department of Trade and Commerce is allegedly, and I believe in fact, engaged in securing markets, a very strong campaign is being waged all over Canada to induce Canadians to send overseas Danish products which will come into competition sooner or later with Canadian products. I have before me an advertisement in a recent issue of the Regina Leader that shows the extent to which this matter is being followed up in parts of the country. I will not refer to the name of the company; I will send the advertisement over to the minister.-It reads:
_ Choice of two Christmas parcels for British isles: Renowned Danish quality products packed in Copenhagen and sent by airmail, delivered within sixteen days of order. Order now. Package No. 1: two pounds butter, one pound cheese, one and seven-eighths pounds canned meat, $7.
Then package No. 2:
Two pounds butter, one pound cheese, one and seven-eighths pounds tongue.
It is the same as the other order, with this added, "Two pounds bacon" and the total is $9.45. In other words, Canadians are asked to buy Danish products to be sent to Britain to relieve the situation over there, and for two pounds bacon, including cost of transportation, one pays $2.45. Does that indicate the type of prices that are being paid to-day on the continent, profiteering that is taking place^ in this country by companies engaged in this kind of work?

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have the minister on his feet anyway now. We have not heard from him for quite a while. We are endangering our agricultural markets in connection with these products by Canadians being asked to send or permit companies to send Danish farm products into Britain, and I am asking whether or not a concerted effort is being made by the department to permit of Canadians sending Canadian farm products over there to relieve the ration situation. There are other parcels indicated which can be sent to Czechoslovakia, Finland, Holland and Scandinavia and the prices are on a par with those I have mentioned. There are still other types of parcels for transmission to Belgium, France and Holland. This has become a racket across the country, and I am surprised that the minister has not seen them because they can be found in the papers all across the country.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Who is responsible for the advertising?

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The companies that are going to make money at the expense of Canadians in Canada and probably at the expense of future Canadian trade abroad. Surely something can be done to prevent this kind of thing. I believe it was stopped once before and I think it should be stopped now. It is a serious thing if we in Canada send Canadian dollars abroad for the purpose of buying Danish farm products to be sent into Britain in competition with, or in substitution of Canadian products. I suggest that the minister should db something at once with regard to this matter.
I pass to one other matter, namely, British markets being closed to-day because of the requirements of the government of Great Britain that import licences be taken out or that Canadian industries establish themselves in the old country. That is a serious blow at empire unity, at commonwealth unity, at commonwealth trade, and to British preferences. The minister should give a statement as to what the Canadian government is doing with reference to the plan being adopted by the British government. If this policy is followed1, to what extent during the next year or two will it mean a reduction in exports from Canada to Great Britain of the products of

Supply-Trade and Commerce
the companies which will be required to establish themselves in the United Kingdom under this policy? What types of manufacturers are precluded from establishing in Britain? What type of companies in Canada will have to establish their factories over there, and to what extent will production in Canada be reduced by the denial of the British market? It is a serious matter when, one part of the British commonwealth establishes, during the existence of British preference regulations, laws or orders which prevent imports from another part of the empire subject to the British preference.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
May I say a few words
before the minister replies to the many questions that have been raised. The question of trade is a thorny one. It is a subject that has been the theme of debate in many political battles in the Dominion of Canada. To-night some hon. members referred to their younger days. Although I am not very old, I can well remember when free trade versus protection was the stock issue in every political fight all across Canada. In these days, that issue has given place to unemployment, family allowances, unemployment insurance, health insurance, and all that sort of thing. My feeling in regard to trade and the tariff question is that the Conservatives believed in a high tariff that was not too high, and the Liberals believed in a low tariff that was not too low: but generally the tariff remained the same, no matter which party was in office. In a recent issue of the Commercial Intelligence Journal I was glad to note how quickly the trade of Canada had picked up on the ending of hostilities. There is a reason for that, and I believe it is one that Canadians must keep in mind in our trade and commercial relations with peoples in other parts of the world. The reason, of course, is that Canada and the United States, of the great trading nations of the world, were the only two countries that came out of this war with their productive facilities greatly enlarged over what they had been when they went into the war.
At the moment we are at an advantage in getting our exports into the markets of the world. We should not be too greedy in taking advantage of that. The hon. member for Davenport, who is not at the moment in his seat, asked the minister what he was doing to combat imports into this country. Surely, if we expect to sell, and if we expect the people of Canada to benefit from our export trade, we must buy. It is only in that way that we can raise our standard of living.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I bet his leader would not
raise that question.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am not going into that. Let us remember, too, that as we find markets, and particularly markets for industrial machinery, in other parts of the world, we are paving the way for a reduction in our export trade as soon as these countries became self-sufficient. They will not stop there; they, too, will begin looking for trade in other parts of the world and they will become our competitors. Therefore there is only one solution of our problem- cooperation in the matter of trade.
A question was raised in regard to the action of the British government in imposing licences on imports from Canada. It has been said that that is a blow at the Ottawa agreements or trade preferences. Surely we should keep in mind that Britain lost almost all her export trade during the war. She put everything she had into the war. If they are now brought to the point where they have to impose restrictions on imports it amounts to this, that to-day Great Britain has to choose between imports that are essential to the life of her people and luxury imports. If she must have steel, oil, or certain essential metals, then she is going to have those instead of fur coats, diamonds, and that sort of thing. Is there any man in this house who will blame her for doing that? Is there any man in this house who would say that Canada would not do the same thing if she were in the same position? These are matters that we should keep in mind.
With the successful negotiation of the loan from the United States and perhaps another loan from the Dominion of Canada, maybe the United Kingdom can get her trade on a normal basis within a short period of time. We should continually keep in mind the condition to which the trade of the United Kingdom was reduced during six years of war, and the necessity for the government, of that country being concerned with the import of those things that are essential to the life of the people, before exporters in other parts of the world proceed to dump on them anything they may have to sell.

speechtext: I think it is a pity that anyone should get the impression that I got from the reading, by the hon. member for Lake Centre, of an advertisement he has taken from what appears to 'be a Winnipeg paper. I may be wrong in that; however, it is a Canadian paper.

Winnipeg. It is endeavouring to get Canadians to place orders in Copenhagen for shipments of goods from Denmark to England. It is possible that some action might be taken in Canada to prevent an advertisement of that kind, but the impression I got from the hon. member's speech and from his reference to the advertisement was one which, I believe, is different from that which he would want to give the country at large. I do not believe any Canadian authority is to blame in this connection.
The hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the British preference, and asked that a full statement be made on the matter. I anticipated that when my estimates would be under consideration questions would be asked about the British preference, Bretton Woods, trade and kindred matters. But may I point out that for a considerable length of time in the house these matters have been under discussion as a result of bills introduced by the Minister of Finance, the minister directly responsible. There has been an attempt in Canada-not to-night-to make the negotiations recently concluded in Washington appear to have been trade discussions or trade agreements. The fact is that the discussions at Washington, in which delegations from the United Kingdom and the United States took part, were financial. Trade conversations were only incidental; and they were conversations only, and not negotiations. Canada is not bound in that connection by anything that took place at Washington, and, besides this, these preliminary negotiations are confidential.
The next step in connection with Great Britain's efforts to put her economy on a sound basis will be, I should imagine, the loan-discussions with Canada which, I may say, will proceed shortly, and will be followed at a later date by trade discussions between Canada and the United Kingdom, possibly in Ottawa and London. It may be a matter of weeks-possibly a few months-before those trade discussions can take place. Meantime I am urging that steps be taken to make some temporary arrangements with the United1 Kingdom to be effective until our trade negotiations can take place. It is impossible for me to give any prolonged statement respecting negotiations and discussions between Canada and the United Kingdom, as suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre, because, as I have said, they are only starting.

He will know that the people of Latin-America are anxious to trade with us, and that we stand very highly in those countries. Our goods have a reputation for high quality, reliability and dependability.
While we have not nearly as large a representation in those countries from my department or from the Department of External Affairs as have the United States or the United Kingdom, man for man I would put our trade commissioners up against those of the representatives of those other two countries.
The hon. member for Peterborough West referred to the fact that trade inquiries had been dropped from the Commercial Intelligence Journal. He is right, but I may say that a decision was arrived at recently to resume the publication of those figures and they will appear in the next issue, or very shortly in any event.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, referred to some matters in an interesting manner and with personal knowledge, but I think these are largely outside the Department of Trade and Commerce. I do not know whether the hon. member for Yorkton wants me to go farther into the announcements on wheat prices; that is the $1.55 price. It is not a ceiling price because there is no such thing as that; it is the price of our export wheat.

The wheat programme and the wheat policy for next year will not be announced until after the New Year, following the usual custom. At that time the policy of. the department and of the government will be made public. speechtext: The minister said a few moments ago that tied up with the present export price of $1.55 is a guarantee that wheat will not be sold below $1 a bushel for the next five years, but he forgot to tell us that since the war for quite a while we have taken seventy cents f.o.b. Fort William for the best grain grown in the world. By so doing, the farmers suffered a distinct loss during all those years until 1942, when we were given an initial price of ninety cents a bushel. The minister also forgot to tell us that during those years the farmers of Canada had to stand the expense of interest on the money borrowed to advance to the farmers on the grain sold and also vast amounts in storage, for the elevators all over the country were full. All those charges were piled on the Canadian farmers and should properly have been a charge on the Canadian people as a whole. If the government wants to treat the farmers at least half fairly that price of $1 a bushel up to the end of July, 1950, should be increased to SI.25, the present initial price. If these charges were laid on the Canadian people as a whole it would give the farmers a chance to become reestablished and encourage them to work with a little more heart and courage even under present conditions.

I wish to say a few words with reference to the coastwise service on the British Columbia coast, especially from Vancouver north. I should like to see the department take an interest in trying to promote a better mail service to many of the points up the coast. I can give one example, of the village of Bella Coola, which is a good farming centre, but it has only one boat a week from Vancouver; if it could have a better service I am sure that that valley would grow, because there are great possibilities, especially in the future when it becomes hooked up with the interior.
I should also like the department to take an interest in seeing that better boats are provided for the service to the Queen Charlotte islands. The boats used now by the Union Steamship company are nothing more than perambulating junk-heaps, and it is no pleasure to ride on them. I have worked on them, and I pity the sailor who works on them. Quite often the passengers have to swim around for their shoes. That is actually what is happening. It does not make for the growth of Queen Charlotte islands settlements such as Massett and Queen Charlotte city.
I wish to bring another matter to the attention of the minister now, so that it -may be on the record and I can criticize him in future years if needs be. In 1939, by order in council 1280, dated May 31, the government allowed a subsidy of $6,750 per sailing for two boats, for experimental sailings out of the port of Prince Rupert. That was cancelled owing to the imminence of the war. Now that the war is over, the port is in far

Supply-Trade and Commerce
better condition to handle these boats because of increased facilities there consequent upon the growth that took place during the war.
I should like to see the government promote that actively as soon as possible. Ships will be released from the pools in the near future, and when normal shipping relations are established once more I should like to see the port get a start as peace-time trade increases. We are looking for action from the government in the near future, because the whole north has to depend upon this. It is part of the general hook-up of the railway situation all through that country, and this subsidizing and supporting of deep-sea sailings out of the port of Prince Rupert will have its effect on the whole north. We know that in the past trade has been able to start by itself, but we recognize now that the state has to interfere actively and to take the lead in sponsoring such things, and Prince Rupert is looking to the department to do this for them.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Are there no plans made for the work that is to be done by the travel bureau? This is the organization which is responsible for the promotion of tourist business.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I have no doubt that a great deal of consideration has been given to plans for the post-war period. I would suggest to the minister that he give us more detail as to what plans have been made. This is one of the most important industries in Canada.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:

I am quite sure he. will realize, however, that, this matter having just come into the department, I am not now in a position to make an extended statement. As I intimated, there will be some supplementary estimates brought down, at which time I would be ready to make a statement.
However, I can say now that the regular work of the branch has been proceeded with and preparations made for extensive advertising throughout foreign countries, particularly the United States and Latin-American countries, respecting the great tourist, attractions we have in Canada, Money has been appropriated for the preparation of literature advertising those resources.
We are also planning a campaign which will have for its purpose that of making the people of Canada individually realize the importance of this tourist business, so that when people come to Canada they may be taken care of properly and courteously, in order that they may be good travelling ambassadors for Canadian scenery.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
There is one matter concerning which I should like to ask the minister a few questions. It has to do with the recent action in Windsor, Ontario, where a convicted robber was given the test by a lie detector. That, I believe, is the first time in the history of this country that anything along that line has been attempted, or that it has been used for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not those convicted have been in fact guilty of any offence.
In this connection I would ask the minister the circumstances under which the test was made upon the convict, and whether or not tests by lie detectors have now become sufficiently scientifically advanced as to be reasonably infallible.
The convict in question had been sentenced to a period of twelve years in prison. Ho appealed, and his appeal was dismissed. He escaped from gaol while awaiting the hearing of the appeal, and returned to custody under an arrangement whereby he was to have

Supply-Justice
applied to him the lie detector with a view to ascertaining whether or not he had in fact committed the offence of which he had- denied commission.
Having read of this case, I looked up as well as I could some of the methods being used in this connection, to ascertain wdiether there was any foundation for what was done in this case. I find that there are several appliances being used, more particularly in Michigan, which adjoins the city of Windsor. There, many innocent persons who have been sentenced to imprisonment have been cleared, as a result of the examinations which have taken place through the use of what is known as a polygraph machine. It is known as the Keeler polygraph.
I am referring now to the London Spectator wherein it is stated that this machine is seventy-five per cent accurate, and that another machine known as the Summers pathometer, which it is claimed demonstrates a lie by means of a variation in the electrical resistance of the skin to an electric current, is supposed to detect ninety-eight per cent of guilty persons and 100 per cent of the innocent.
I know of no advance made in recent years that could be more important than this one.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Does the hon. member believe in it?

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
That is not for
me to say. After all. the law is always far behind scientific development. It took many years before finger-printing was accepted, and many years before criminology would permit of the taking of evidence in connection with firearms, the identification of cartridges, and the like.
Whether I believe in it or not, this was actually tried out in the Windsor case. According to press reports the man was found to have been innocent of the offence for which he had been sentenced and was about to serve a long term of imprisonment.
Is this system to be applied generally throughout the country, and in particular in penitentiaries where there are men who claim they' are innocent and have been wrongly convicted? Of course one finds that in all penal institutions. The principle has been accepted in this case.
I should like to ask the minister these questions before dealing with the matter any further. First, did that examination take place with the knowledge or consent of the Department of Justice? Did it take place after consideration had been given to the whole question of the reliability of the lie detector device?
This is important because, if there has been no evidence to support the accuracy of the lie detector, then it should not have been used in that case, because it leads people to believe that this man is wrongfully serving a sentence. If, on the other hand, it has been accepted byr the Department of Justice as a result of examination as being reasonably infallible, then I submit that the time has come when it should be generally applied throughout the penal institutions of this country.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The answer to the first question is, no. The answer to the second question is that the Department of Justice does not know anything at all about it. The answer to the third question is that the Department of Justice does not attempt in the penitentiaries to ascertain whether convictions pronounced in the courts charged with the administration of justice are proper or not.

maintopic: VETERANS' LAND ACT IN CORPORATION OF PROVISIONS OF CERTAIN ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Why then was this examination allowed of a man who had received a sentence to the penitentiary?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon, member will have to address his question to the attorney general of Ontario who has to do with the administration of justice in this province. The Department of Justice had nothing whatsoever to do with the incident to which the hon. member refers.
